The days are: Pratipada to Agni, second to Brahma, third to the lord of wealth, fourth to Ganesha, fifth to the serpent king, sixth to Kartikeya, seventh to the sun, eighth to Rudra, ninth to Durga, tenth to Yama, eleventh to the Vishvedevas, twelfth to Vishnu, thirteenth to Kamadeva, fourteenth to Shiva, the full moon to Soma, and the new moon to the fathers. Each brings its own reward for worship, such as learning, wealth, success in business, freedom from snake poison, long life, victory and sons. Brahma then lists the gods of the 27 stars and what worship under each gives (for example Ashvins long life, Yama protection from untimely death, Agni and Prajapati, Soma, Rudra, Aditi, Brihaspati, the snakes, the fathers, Pusha, Bhaga, Savita, Tvashta, Vayu, Indra-Agni, Mitra, Indra, Vishnu, the Vasus, Aja and Pusha) and says that worship by star and day brings all success in journeys and acts, and that worship of the sun leads to freedom.

01-103.json.summary: Brahma tells Krishna the rewards of serving the sun. One who builds a lasting temple of the sun lifts seven generations to the sun's world, and enjoys the sun's world for as many thousand years as the image stays in the temple. Flowers, incense, lamps and offerings given daily to the sun, even durva grass shoots, give fruit that is hard to win by sacrifices. Krishna asks how fasts please the sun and how a faster should serve him. Brahma says the sun helps those who enjoy offerings, so much more those who fast: fasting means turning away from sin and from all enjoyment; one, two or three nights of fasting, thinking of the sun with devotion, desireless, brings the highest Brahman, and a fast held with a wish brings that wish. All classes and women, stuck in the mud of worldly life, can reach a good end by worshipping him; a man with a mind on sense objects cannot. If flowers are lacking, leaves or durva shoots will do. Sweeping the temple frees from sin and gives as many divine days in heaven as there are dust grains swept; plastering, sprinkling water, giving lamps, a banner, a pot of sesame, singing, music and reading sacred stories each bring named rewards. One bow to the sun equals the bath after ten horse sacrifices. The sun is the one god for every stage of life and every class; Shiva, freed from the sin of killing a Brahmin, and others gained their state through him.

01-104.json.summary: Brahma goes on to describe fasts for particular wishes. On the bright seventh of Phalguna one repeats the name "Heli" many times (108 times at worship, and also at travelling, rising, stumbling and sneezing), avoids heretics, outcastes and unjust people, and prays to the sun, the "swan", to rescue those sunk in the sea of life. He fasts, eats once in the morning, bathes, and worships again, doing the same in Chaitra, Vaishakha and Jyeshtha. In Ashadha, Shravana, Bhadrapada and Ashvina he does the same, repeating "Martanda" and drinking cow's urine; and from Kartika for four months he drinks milk and repeats "Bhaskara". Each month he gives gifts to Brahmins, and at the end of the four-month period he has a Purana or the story of the sun read, honours the reader, and holds a Shraddha. The three breakings of the fast give property and rule, the sun's world, and then the highest state, for women as well as men. Hearing or reading this removes sin.

01-105.json.summary: Brahma explains another Saptami, on the bright seventh of Phalguna. The worshipper fasts, repeats the sun's name, eats little and speaks of the sun even when rising and sleeping. The next day, the eighth, he bathes, worships, gives a fee to a Brahmin, makes a ghee offering in fire, and says a prayer asking for his wishes, naming Savitri, who once won her wish by worshipping the sun, and Indra, who regained his kingdom through him. The fast is broken in four stages of four months, each with its own flowers, incense and food: karavira flowers and kasara in Phalguna to Jyeshtha, jasmine and rice pudding from Ashadha, red lotuses and cow's urine from Kartika, with "Mahanga" incense of camphor, sandalwood, mustaka, aguru, tagara, pepper, sugar and sihlaka. One must not be mean with money. Those who kept it were Indra (gaining the three worlds), Savitri, Aditi, the Yadavas, Dhaumya, Krishna himself (as Bhargavi's gain), Shankara and Brahma. It gives sons to the childless, health to the sick, a husband to a maiden, and the sun's world, then rule as a king on earth.

01-106.json.summary: Brahma tells Krishna more of what the sun told the bird (Aruna) about the merit of lunar days. Krishna asks about Vijaya, Atijaya and Jayanti and the northern course (uttarayana). Brahma says the bright seventh joined with the sun's own star (Hasta) is very meritorious; worship on it frees from sin of seven births, fasting frees from all sin, and anything given or offered is never lost. Repeating one Rigveda verse before the sun gives the fruit of the whole Rigveda, and the same for the Sama, Yajur and Atharva Vedas. The worshipper shines like the stars, then goes in a camphor car to the sun's city, bright as Shukra and the sun, and returns to earth as a king.

01-107.json.summary: Brahma tells Krishna about the sun's two feet, the southern and northern courses of the sun. The right foot is the southern course (dakshinayana) and the left, Vamana's, the northern (uttarayana). Brahma and Krishna worship the right foot, and Vishnu and Shiva the left. Krishna asks how to worship. Brahma says in the northern course one bathes the sun with ghee and milk, offers cloth, flowers, incense and paste, and feeds Brahmins. Then one takes a six-month vow: to say the sun's name each day, whatever one does (eating, walking, sleeping, waking, bowing, offering, even at a stumble or start of Vedic study), and to be aware that if one dies within six months the sun is the goal. After six months one pleases the sun as one can, feeds Brahmins with fees, has a sacred story read before the sun, and honours the reader and the writer. This frees from all sin; death during the six months gives the fruit of a fast unto death. The sun once told this to the moon who asked.

01-108.json.summary: Brahma tells Krishna about the Sarvapti Saptami, the dark seventh of Magha, which gives every wish. The worshipper bows, does not talk to heretics, and worships with a single mind. The fast is broken in six two-month stages, one for each of the months starting with Magha, with the sun addressed as Martanda, Ka, Chitrabhanu, Vibhavasu, Bhaga and Hamsa. At the end of each, the five cow products are used for bathing and drinking, the worshipper bows, gives a fee, and honours the sun. He eats at night, avoids oil and alkali, and keeps watch on the night or day of the Saptami. It frees from all sin and gives all wishes, which is why it is famed as the seventh that gets everything. Brahma tells Krishna to worship the sun as Bhaganadhipati did long ago.

01-109.json.summary: Brahma tells Krishna the Martanda Saptami, kept on the bright seventh of Pausha. One fasts, worships the sun, and repeats "Martanda" (also on sleeping, waking or stumbling), worships the kutapa (the noon hour or its offering) with incense and flowers, gives a fee to a Brahmin, and avoids heretics. To purify himself he takes cow's urine, milk, curds or other cow products. The next day he bathes, worships again under the same name, gives a fee, and eats food made with milk. He keeps this every month, giving a cow or other gift to Brahmins monthly, and at the year's end gives a larger gift: a cow with gold-tipped horns on the fifth and a bull on the sixth. It brings the sun's world and a body as bright as the sage Shandileya. Brahma says the heavenly hosts who kept it are still seen shining, and tells Krishna to worship the sun in this way.

01-110.json.summary: Brahma describes the Saptami of Bhadrapada's bright half. One bows to the seven-horsed sun, worships with flowers and incense and the offering to the kutapa hour, avoids heretics and eats at night in silence, repeating the sun's name even when standing, walking, sneezing or stumbling. After twelve months, at the end of the breaking of the fast, one worships the sun and gains the fruit of the Shravana (Shravana-month) rite, which is endless. It gives rich enjoyment, dharma and wealth here, and the sun's world after death, also for women.

01-111.json.summary: Brahma describes the Saptami of Shravana's bright half. The worshipper is clean, bows, worships the sun with flowers and incense, does not speak with heretics, gives a fee to a Brahmin and eats at night in silence. Every year he gives the sun an oil anointing (abhyanga) on this Saptami, with new white rice, and music is played; he feeds Brahmins with conch and drum sounds and Vedic chanting. After twelve months and the end of the fast, a fee is given to a Brahmin. The worshipper rides a heavenly car to the sun's world, and reaches the heaven of the one in the forest garland (Vishnu).

01-112.json.summary: Brahma tells Krishna that the sun, even when worshipped with water, gives rewards hard to win, but he is pleased by a pure heart, not by killing animals, flowers or fruits. The heart must be free from desire, speech free from lies, and deeds free from harm; one with an impure heart is bound by the sun in the mud, and darkness does not leave him. One who gives all he has with a crooked mind does not truly worship him; so Krishna should give the sun a heart free from passion. Krishna then asks what gives good birth, health and wealth. Brahma says: on the bright seventh of Magha with the Hasta star, one fasts, worships the sun with fragrance, and keeps this for a year, giving to Brahmins such things as a thunderbolt-shaped gift, sesame, rice, barley, gold, water, a stick, sandals, an umbrella and sweets in order. Month by month one drinks cow's urine, water, sauce, vegetables, durva, curds, grains, sesame, barley, sun-warmed water and milk. The fruit is birth in a great, wealthy family, whole senses, health and wisdom, and Brahma tells Krishna to worship the sun as he does.

01-113.json.summary: Krishna asks Brahma what comes of building a temple for the sun, making his image, anointing, offerings of flowers and incense, song, music, and bathing with ghee and milk. Brahma says that building a temple of wood, stone or clay gives the fruit of a sacrifice every day, lifts a hundred future and a hundred past generations to the sun's world, destroys the sin of seven births from the day work begins, and gives a stay in heaven for as many thousand years as the bricks last. Making an image with the right signs gives the sun's world, sixty thousand times a thousand years of joy; setting up the image in a good place frees from fault and saves all of one's family, past and future, to the end of the age. Brahma then tells how Yama told his messengers, with noose and rod, to leave alone anyone who worships the sun, remembers him when stumbling or sneezing, honours him with flowers and incense, sweeps or plasters his temple, or built one, and to avoid their families. The messengers once ignored this and went to Satrajit, a devotee, and were struck down by his glow like birds knocked from a tree. This is the great reward of building his temple and of worshipping him.

01-114.json.summary: Brahma tells Krishna that a worshipper who properly honours an installed image of the sun gets whatever he wishes. Bathing the image with ghee equals giving a hundred cows, and bathing it with ghee on the dark eighth, or with cow products on the sixth or seventh, destroys great sins; a ghee bath at dusk washes away sins done knowingly or not. King Bhuridyumna is said to have won the earth of seven continents by bathing the image with a pot of water. A milk bath brings joy, health, beauty for seven births, clear knowledge, and the favour of the planets, and the sun is pleased at the mere sight of an image bathed in ghee and milk.

01-115.json.summary: Brahma tells of a talk in heaven between a Brahmin woman, Gautami, and Kaushalya. Gautami, amazed at the beauty of Kaushalya and her husband, asks what austerity, gift or fire offering gave them such scent, glow, clothes and ornaments. Kaushalya answers that they once pleased the sun: bathing him with holy water and perfumes gave their glow, ghee bathing gave a calm mind and charm, and the clothes, jewels, garlands, food and fragrance they offered returned to them. She adds that those who offer without desire for reward are given liberation. Brahma then lists what to offer: sandalwood, aloe, camphor, saffron, incense, many named flowers and leaves that please the sun, flowers to avoid (some give fear, disease and poverty), cloths, foods, fruits, gold, gems and fees, and says to give them all to the sun, thinking of oneself as the sun.

01-116.json.summary: Brahma tells Krishna of King Satrajit, a mighty world emperor and devoted worshipper of the sun, who wonders how he gained his wealth and asks sages at the urging of his wife. The sage Paravasu, using yoga, recalls his past life: he was a low-class man, sick, harsh and poor, with a loyal wife; ruined, he took work, and the two served the sun's temple at Kanyakubja by sweeping, sprinkling, smearing it with dung and clay, lighting a lamp with their own food-oil and the wife's cloth, and having the Itihasa and Purana read. Seeing King Kuvalashva's splendour, he longed for it, and was reborn as a king. The sage teaches that the sun is pleased by sincere feeling rather than costly gifts, and describes month-long vows in Kartika, Margashira and Pausha (one meal a day, the second meal given to a Brahmin), which remove sins of youth, middle age and old age, so that the vow lasts three months or years. Satrajit, glad, asks what the sun likes, and the chapter ends with the sun's words to Aruna: red oleander flowers, red sandalwood, guggulu incense, sweet cakes, a ghee lamp, gifts to the reciter and respect for the Purana reciter, who is dear to him.

01-117.json.summary: Aruna asks the sun why the "bhojaka" priest is dear to him and who he is. The sun explains that he made them from his own body for his worship: King Priyavrata's son in Shakadvipa had a temple and a golden image made but could find no one to install it among the three non-Brahmin classes there. The sun created eight shining sons who read the Vedas, and told the king to have them install the image and give them all the temple's property; those who take it from them go to hell. He lays down the bhojaka's rules: study the Vedas, marry, anoint with oil, bathe three times a day, worship five times, never insult gods, Brahmins or the Vedas, avoid food of Shudras and offered food, blow the conch, keep a shaved head with a tuft, fast on Sundays, the sixth and seventh, speak only good words, bathe the image carefully, never sell or give the offered flowers to Shudras, and give offerings only to Brahmins. The sun threatens to destroy the family of one who insults a bhojaka. Brahma ends by saying the king, hearing his past deed, was glad, had every sun temple he saw cleaned, and his wife paid a reader to recite the Purana there, so both reached the highest state.

01-118.json.summary: Brahma explains that giving a lamp in a sun temple, above all in Kartika, gives the fruit of all sacrifices. He tells of Bhadra, youngest of a hundred sons of the Brahmin Nagasharma of Mahishmati, who kept a thousand lamps burning day and night at the sun's temple. His brothers ask why, and he tells his past: he was once a leprous Shudra living in the temple of the sun built by Vashishtha, the priest of King Ikshvaku, on the Sarayu. One night, with an evil mind, he lit a lamp with a wick to steal the sun's jewel while the temple servants slept, but they caught him, spared him, and royal guards seized him; he died of fear and illness and went to the sun's world, staying a kalpa. By the merit of that lamp he was reborn a learned Brahmin who remembers his past life. Brahma lists the rewards of giving lamps in Kartika: memory of past lives, wisdom, sound senses, good sight, and a golden lamp-garlanded heavenly car; one who steals lamps is reborn a mouse or blind.

01-119.json.summary: Brahma continues the lamp story. A servant of Yama speaks to sinners crying in the dark hell: lamenting is useless, since they neglected their own good, and human life is brief and sense pleasures weak. He urges them to avoid sin and to worship the sun always, since this removes sin done through ignorance. The tormented, parched sinners ask what they did, and he tells them they stole a lamp from the sun's house in their youth for the ghee, and so fell into this hell of hunger, thirst and cold wind. Brahma closes that giving lamps is praised everywhere, most of all in the sun's temple, and lamps are carried away only by the blind, dumb and foolish.

01-120.json.summary: Krishna asks why beings suffer from poison, disease, evil planets and spells, and Brahma says it comes from not having pleased the sun in earlier lives, while one who pleases him gets health, wealth, safe planets and protection from enemies. Krishna asks how to worship him and wishes to become strong; Brahma tells him to become "Vaivasvata", a devotee of the sun, and describes the kind of man this is: harmless in deed, thought and word, honouring bhojakas, Brahmins and gods, seeing everything as the sun's, devoted and free of hatred; those who scorn the sun and the Vedas have an asura share. He promises long stay in the flower-house for those who build a temple or image, tells Krishna to offer flowers, incense, lamps, red clothes, food and holy-water, ghee and milk baths, hymns, music and gifts to Brahmins, and says even durva shoots offered with love give fruit better than sacrifices. Brahma says he himself came from the sun's right ray, Shiva from the left, Vishnu from his chest, and that by worship he gained strength and fame. One who hears this talk gets his wishes.

01-121.json.summary: Someone asks to hear in detail about the "drawing of the sun's body" mentioned briefly before. The story tells that when Samjna went to her father's house, the sun thought of making a form like hers; Brahma came, praised the sun, and told Vishvakarma, the sun's father-in-law, to shape him. Vishvakarma slowly made the sun's form, putting him on the earth. As it was drawn, Brahma, Shiva, Vishnu, Indra, seven sages led by Vishvamitra, the Valakhilyas, vidyadharas, yakshas, nagas, gandharvas and apsaras praised him with hymns, music and dance, and all gods bowed. Vishvakarma meanwhile gradually trimmed down the sun's glow. A closing verse says hearing this leads to the sun's world at the end of life.

01-122.json.summary: Shatanika asks how the sun was praised by Brahma and the gods at the time his body was being drawn. Sumantu answers with a hymn of salutations to the sun: the lord of the sky, who opens the lotuses, removes the cloth of darkness, grants wishes, is unborn, the soul of beings, the eye of all the worlds, and has a thousand rays. The chapter says Brahma, Shiva, Vishnu and the other gods praised him this way long ago.

01-123.json.summary: Shatanika asks for more sun stories, and Sumantu retells what Brahma said. Burned by the sun's rays, sages ask Brahma in his world who this blazing being is. Brahma tells how, in the dark before creation, mind, ego, the great elements and the cosmic egg arose, and he, Vishnu and Shiva, dazed by darkness, meditated and the dark-removing light broke forth; they praised him as the first god, the one who is Brahma, Shiva, Vishnu, time, and the highest self. Pleased, the sun offers a boon, and they ask that his glare be made bearable; he agrees. The text says meditators and seekers of liberation meditate on the sun, and that fire offerings and sacrifices equal not even a sixteenth part of devotion to him. Then the gods praise him again, and Vishvakarma, by Brahma's order, puts the sun on a lathe and slowly trims off his glow; the sun does not like being drawn, but his feet stay covered since then. From the trimmed glow came Vishnu's discus, Shiva's trident, Skanda's spear, Kubera's palanquin, and weapons for the gods. Reading this hymn at both twilights cleanses the family, and the chapter ends with the sun finding Samjna in mare form in the northern Kuru land; hearing it is said to equal a horse sacrifice.

01-124.json.summary: Brahma tells the sages about the sun's chief attendants. Shiva, naked and carrying a skull after beheading Brahma, wanders, and the forest sages' wives and daughters are stirred; his attendants tell him to stand before the sun, who will cleanse him. The sun, pleased, names him Dindi. Brahma then lists the sun's eighteen chief attendants and others who ride with him, each explained by the roots of their names: Dandanayaka (Skanda), Pingala (fire), the two Ashvins, door-keepers Rajna and Srausha, Kalmasha (Yama) and the bird Garuda, Kubera and Vinayaka, Raivata and Dindi. They stand around the sun to guard him against the demons. Sumantu closes by saying those sages worshipped the sun and now live in heaven.

01-125.json.summary: Shatanika asks about the "vyoma", the structure seen before the sun, and Sumantu explains it as the sun's four-horned weapon, like Varuna's noose, Vishnu's discus, Shiva's trident or Indra's thunderbolt, in which thirty-three gods live. He lists the gods in it: eleven Rudras, twelve Adityas, eight Vasus, two Ashvins, ten Vishvadevas and twelve Sadhyas, then the fourteen Manus and Indras, the seven sages, the Maruts, three fires, the five year-gods and the fathers, and the nine planets (Sun, Moon, Mars, Mercury, Jupiter, Venus, Saturn, Rahu, Ketu) with their parents, order, and sizes. He sets out the seven worlds from Bhur to Satya, the heights above earth, and the eight kinds of divine beings. Worshipping this vyoma worships all gods, and the devotee reaches Shiva's world.

01-126.json.summary: The chapter gives names and layout of the sky and the earth. It lists synonyms for the sky, the seven oceans (salt, milk, curds, sour, ghee, honey-sugar-cane, sweet water), six year-mountains such as Himavan and Nishadha, the central silver mountain, and the eight directional cities. Then it lists the seven upper worlds, the seven lower ones (Atala to Rasatala), and the layered coverings of the cosmic egg, each wrapped by fire, air, sky, ego, nature and spirit, all covered by the Lord, the sun. Mount Meru is described as golden and four-sided, 84,000 yojanas tall, with four peaks, Saumanasa, Jyotishka, Chitra and Chandraujaska, from which the sun rises. It names the gods standing on each peak (Venus, Saturn, Kubera, Moon, Shiva and others), with Brahma in the middle, and says Meru is the sky, dharma and the Vedas, its four peaks the four Vedas.

01-127.json.summary: Shatanika asks how Samba, Krishna's son, pleased the sun and was freed of disease. Sumantu tells it: after hearing the sun's greatness from Narada, the sick Samba asks his father Krishna for leave, goes to the Mitravana on the Chandrabhaga river, fasts, and recites a secret hymn praising the sun as Vishnu, Brahma, Rudra, Indra, time, and the healer of white leprosy, blindness, deafness and lameness. The sun, pleased, offers a boon. Samba asks first for deep devotion, then that the dirt and disease in his body vanish; the sun grants it and he sheds the illness like a snake its skin and takes a divine form. The sun adds that shrines set up in his name will give rewards, tells Samba to install him on the Chandrabhaga, promises the place will be called by his name, and ends by promising dream visions. The hymn, read three times a day or used in a seven-night fire offering, brings kingdoms, wealth or health.

01-128.json.summary: The sun appears to Samba in a dream when he is thin and tired after a thousand-name praise, and tells him to drop the thousand names and say a short hymn instead. He gives twenty-one secret names, including Vaikartana, Vivasvan, Martanda, Bhaskara, Ravi, Lokaprakashaka, Tapana and Saptashvavahana. This "king of hymns" gives health, wealth and fame and frees from all sin if spoken at dawn and dusk; one recital before him destroys wrong done by mind, speech or body, and it serves as a prayer, fire offering, twilight rite, and offering mantra. The sun vanishes, and Samba is healed.

01-129.json.summary: Samba, now healed, goes with other ascetics to bathe in the Chandrabhaga and thinks about what image of the sun to set up. He sees a shining image of the sun floating in the river current, takes it out, and installs it in the Mitravana. He asks the image who made it. It answers that when the sun's old form was too bright to bear, Brahma and the gods asked for a milder one, and Vishvakarma shaped him on a lathe in Shakadvipa; he had this image made from a wishing tree, set on the Himalaya's back, and sent down the Chandrabhaga for Samba's sake. The sun says he will be present here, seen in the morning, noon and afternoon, worshipped by Brahma in the morning, by Vishnu at noon and by Shiva in the afternoon, and then disappears.

01-130.json.summary: A question opens the chapter: how did Samba have the sun installed and a temple built? The reply (speaker not named in the text) says that after finding the image, Samba thought of Narada, who came; Samba asked what reward comes from building a sun temple and installing an image, and where and how to build. Narada says to build near plentiful water, a garden and beautiful places where gods like to stay, and gives a plan of sixty-four squares with a central door, proportions for height, doorway and sanctum, and lists twenty temple types (Meru, Kailasa, Mandara, Vimana, Nandana, Samudga, Padma, Garuda, Nandi, Kunjara, Griharaja, Vrisha, Hamsa, Ghata, Sarvatobhadra, Simha and others) with their sizes. A sun temple is to be built in the middle of a town or in its east. He then explains how to test the soil, dig and fill a pit, and where to place the attendant deities, bathing room, fire-rite room, offering circles, and the "vyoma" and reader's place.

01-131.json.summary: Narada explains how to make an image. There are seven kinds: gold, silver, copper, clay, stone, wood and painted. For a wooden image the maker enters a forest on an auspicious day and takes a tree; he lists trees to avoid (milky trees, those at crossroads, in temples or cremation grounds, struck by weapons or fire, bird-nests, dried tops, and similar), and good ones such as madhuka, deodar, sandalwood, bilva, khadira and neem, with particular trees for Brahmins, Kshatriyas, Vaishyas and Shudras. Before felling, one fasts, anoints the ground, bathes the tree with consecrated water, makes a fire offering, worships it and asks the spirits living in it to move elsewhere, takes an axe in worship, and cuts it the next morning after gifts to Brahmins and bhojakas. The direction in which the tree falls and its sap and leaves are read as good or bad signs.

01-132.json.summary: Narada gives the signs of a good sun image. Its height is one, two, three or three and a half hands, each bringing a different gain (peace, wealth and grain, all wishes, good harvests). Face, nose, eyes, ears, neck, chest, arms, legs and feet are measured in finger-widths; the face is wide, lotus-like, smiling, with a crown, bracelets, earrings and a necklace, holding a golden lotus garland in both hands. Flaws bring harm: a small, damaged, hollow-bellied or thin image brings danger from kings, hunger, poverty, death by weapons or loss of life or a spouse; images tilted or looking up or down also bring bad results. The chapter ends with signs for other gods: Brahma with a water pot and four faces on a lotus, Skanda as a boy with a spear and peacock banner, Indra with four tusks and a thunderbolt, and Shiva with a third eye.

01-133.json.summary: Narada explains the preparing ("adhivasana") of the image: a pavilion in the north-east with four arches, hung with flags of different colours in each direction. Clay images bless all, jewelled ones bring good harvests, silver brings fame, copper brings children, stone brings land, and tin or lead images destroy the leading man. Samba asks why the sun is called "all-gods"; Narada answers that all gods live in his body: Mercury and Moon as eyes, Shiva on the forehead, Jupiter on the skull, the Rudras at the throat, planets and stars in the teeth, Dharma and Adharma in the lips, Sarasvati on the tongue, the sages in the pores, the oceans in the belly, rivers in the arms, mountains in the armpits, Meru on the back, the nether worlds in the nails, and so on. He says this is the highest knowledge and promises to tell the rest of the installation as Brahma told it.

01-134.json.summary: Narada gives the times and set-up for installing the image: lunar days one, two, four, five, ten, thirteen and full moon; the planets Moon, Jupiter, Venus and Mercury; and a list of good constellations. The ground is cleared and a four-hand altar and ten-hand pavilion built, with clay from river meetings, fire pits of different shapes in each direction, four arches of sacred trees with Rig Veda mantras for each, pots with gold inside, wrapped in white sandalwood paste, flags in the colours of each direction guardian, a bed with grass, lamps, sweets, rice-milk, curds, and a white umbrella. The festival is held with conch, bells, music and Vedic chant.

01-135.json.summary: Narada describes the bathing rite. The bathing priest should be a wise Brahmin, learned in the Vedas and in the sun's texts, and Aruna and the bhojakas attend. The image is brought on a seat in procession and bathed with water from the sea, Ganga, Yamuna, Sarasvati, Chandrabhaga, Sindhu, Pushkara and mountain springs, using pots of earth, copper, silver and gold, then with gems, herbs, flowers, sandalwood, pañcagavya (five cow products), milk, curds, ghee, honey and cane juice, each with its Vedic mantra; eight sets of verses invite gods, sages, Indra, nagas, mountains, the seven sages and the Vasus to bathe the sun. The rite then gives the sacred thread, a pair of cloths, a garland, incense, eye-black, and lamp-waving. Bathing it gives the fruit of Agnishtoma, Rajasuya, Ashvamedha and other sacrifices; the bath water must not be stepped on or eaten by crows. The chapter ends with who should and should not be chosen as priest (not deformed, ill, cheating, quarrelsome, a paid astrologer, and so on).

01-136.json.summary: Narada gives the preparing and installing rite. The image is placed in the pavilion on grass, welcomed, offered honey and water and shown a cow and calf; each year in Shravana a new cloth is given. The sacred syllables (om, hum, kha, sha, la, ka, ya, na, ma) are placed on the priest's body and the image, each with a colour to meditate on. Fire offerings follow in four fire pits tended by priests of the four Vedas and a bhojaka in the centre, with offerings of twelve thousand or fewer sticks and the life-cycle rites symbolically done for the image. The image rests for three or five nights or one day on a white bed with Dandi and Pingala at its feet, with night watch, hymns and music. In the morning it is placed on a gold seven-horse chariot in the sanctum, facing straight, with his two wives beside it; offerings go to Indra, Fire, Yama, Nirriti, Varuna, Vayu, Soma, Ishana and the serpents. The rewards listed: the fruit of ten horse sacrifices and a hundred Vajapeyas, health for seven births, and a stay in the sun's world.

01-137.json.summary: Narada closes the section on installation. A man who builds a temple and installs the image gains heavenly joys and lasting fame, and even one who just sees it done reaches heaven. He gives the general installation procedure for all gods: bathe, eat, dress, install on a bed with perfumes and flowers, keep a night watch with song and dance. Hearing the Itihasa and Purana destroys sin and draws the sun's presence, so a reader is honoured, the book is read before the sun, and the installer gives all he has, or a cow, to please the priest. Doing, seeing or hearing this rite brings the sun.

01-138.json.summary: Narada tells Samba how to raise a flag on a sun temple, as Brahma once told it. The flag-pole must be a straight, unbroken bamboo, sized to the temple, with ten kinds named by length: Jaya, Jayanta, Jaitreya, Shatruhanta, Jayavaha, Nanda, Upananda, Indra, Upendra and others; a cracked, bent or short pole brings loss and illness. The cloth banner, ten grades named Ankura, Pallava, Skandha and so on, hangs from it, white, with bells, whisks and a gold, silver or jewelled emblem at the top. Each god has an emblem, pole and banner colour: Vishnu's Garuda with a gold pole and yellow banner, Shiva's bull with silver and white, Brahma's lotus with copper, the sun's Dharma with gold and five colours, Indra's elephant, Yama's buffalo, Varuna's swan or tortoise, Kubera, Balarama's palm, Kama's crocodile, Skanda's peacock, Ganesha's mouse, and others. The pole is consecrated, bathed, kept overnight with offerings, and raised on an auspicious day with a mantra; the direction in which the banner falls shows the world the builder will reach. A temple without a flag draws demons.

01-139.json.summary: Samba, having regained his form, asks who will look after the sun's worship, and Narada says Brahmins do not take what belongs to a god, since doing so makes them unfit temple-priests (devalakas), and sends him to Gauramukha, priest of Ugrasena. Gauramukha refuses the gift for the same reason and says to give the city to the Magas, who alone may worship. He explains the Magas' origin: Nikshubha, daughter of the sage Sujihva, was tending the fire when the sun, desiring her, entered the fire; she crossed it, and the angry fire god told her that Magas would be born of fire. The sage Rigjihva cursed the child to be unworthy of worship, but the sun promised that her son would be learned and his line, learned descendants of Vashishtha, would worship him and her. Samba asks the sun, who tells him to bring his worshippers from Shakadvipa, beyond the salt sea, where the four classes, Maga, Magaga, Mangaga, Mandaga, live free of mixing; the sun lists himself as Vishnu in Jambudvipa, Indra in Shalmali, Bhaga in Krauncha, Bhanu in Plaksha, and so on. Samba flies on Garuda, finds the Magas, and brings eighteen families back to the Mitravana, and the sun is pleased.

01-140.json.summary: Samba founds a city on the Chandrabhaga with the sun installed in its middle, gives it wealth to the bhojakas, and it is called Sambapura. He has Bhoja-family girls married to the Magas, then asks the sun about the Magas' knowledge and is sent to Narada, then to Vyasa. He asks Vyasa a series of questions: who the Magas and bhojakas are, why they are called "divine", why they wear a sacred girdle, keep the sun vow, and recite, what their Vedas and fire rites are. Vyasa, saying the sun has helped his memory, tells what Vasishtha said: the Magas know and act, eat in silence like sages, are called bhojakas from being born of bhoja daughters, and have their own Vedas and name; their oblation rite is the "Adhvahotra", with five incense offerings at three twilights.

01-141.json.summary: Samba asks Vyasa about the bhojakas' girdle, their sacred-thread rite and their class. Vyasa says the eight Magas are the sun's own and the eight Shudras came from his body. Ten Bhoja girls were given to ten of the Magas, and eight Mandaga girls to eight. The sons of the Bhoja girls are called divine Brahmins, and those of slave girls "antya"; the latter are "Madanga" servants of the sun. They worship in Shakadvipa with Vedic mantras. Samba, curious about the sacred cord (avyanga) they wear, asks what it is, where it came from, why it is pure, when it is tied and how long it is; Vyasa promises to explain.

01-142.json.summary: Vyasa explains the avyanga, the sacred belt of the bhojakas. Gods, sages, nagas and others live in the sun by turns; once Vasuki, carrying the sun's chariot for a year, gave him a belt from his own body, bright with the Ganga, and the sun tied it round his middle; for this reason worshippers wear it. One who does not wear it is not fit to worship, loses the reward, and goes to hell. It is single-coloured, of one hundred to a hundred and eight finger-widths, and was made by Vishvakarma; with it the wearer is pure, fire offerings are fruitful, and without it even a rite-purified man is not. Its names are explained by word roots (avyanga, arhaka, sarasana). Brahma sits in its middle, Vishnu at its root, Shiva at its end; the Rig Veda is at the root, Yajur in the middle, Sama at the top; the three worlds sit along it. The chapter ends by promising talk of its binding and the ornaments.

01-143.json.summary: Samba returns to Narada and asks how the bhojakas offer incense, bathing, rinsing the mouth and water offerings to the sun. Narada explains: rinse the mouth correctly, in the right direction and not standing in water, with water drunk three times and parts of the body touched in order, then enter the temple in silence with covered head, worship with flowers, say Gayatri, give incense with guggulu to the fire, and offer a handful of flowers on the sun's head with a Vedic verse. There are five incense times, and three daily worships (morning, noon and evening), each with its own water offering, with copper vessels holding sandalwood water, lotuses, oleander and red lilies. The invocation begins with "come, sun of a thousand rays". Incense is offered to Mihira, Nikshubha, Rajna, Dandanayaka, Pingala, Srausha, the guardians of the directions, Dindi, Shiva, the serpents and others, each with a mantra. Three baths and worship by this rule give the fruit of a horse sacrifice. If flowers are lacking, use leaves, then incense, then water, then a bow, and lastly the mind.

01-144.json.summary: Vyasa goes to Dvaraka to see Krishna, who greets him and asks why the bhojakas, brought by his son from Shakadvipa, are so wise and bound for liberation, and says no one gets freedom without becoming a bhojaka. Vyasa agrees that these devotees of the sun are blessed: they worship him with offerings, herbs and ghee, do the eternal fire offering and a higher offering, and enter the sun's three forms (in fire, in the sky, and in his disc). In the disc is a person who is both perishable and imperishable, with and without parts. Those who follow the Sankhya and yoga paths reach his place, which is liberation. Vyasa explains the syllable "om" as three and a half measures, with "m" being the sun, and says the Magas get their name from meditation on "ma", and bhojakas from feeding the sun with incense, garlands and gifts.

01-145.json.summary: Krishna asks how the bhojakas gain knowledge, and Vyasa answers. The body is bones, sinews, flesh and blood, full of foul things and disease, and should be given up in the mind; a free man has a skull-bowl, tree roots, rags, no companions and sameness toward all beings. He teaches control of the mind and senses, breath control to burn faults like fire, withdrawal, meditation, and cleaning mind by mind. The sun has three forms: red in the morning (Rig Veda, passion), white at noon (Yajur, goodness), black in the evening (Sama, darkness), and a fourth, the sun's disc, that is subtle and spotless. Seated in lotus posture, the yogi cleanses the central channel by breath, sees fire in the navel, moon in the heart and a flame in the head, and pierces the sun's disc to reach the sorrowless supreme place. He says this should be taught only to believers, not to unbelievers. Vyasa then goes to the hermitage of Nara and Narayana at Badari.

01-146.json.summary: Shatanika asks why some bhojakas are called unfit to eat with and what makes them fit. Sumantu tells that Kritavarma once asked Krishna why the sages Narada and Parvata ate at a bhojaka's house in Sambapura if bhojakas were said to be unfit; Krishna answers that bhojakas are not unfit in themselves but become so by bad conduct. Unfit are one who has a low-class wife, does not wear the sacred belt, worships unbathed or without oiling, eats Shudra food, farms, neglects temple worship, skips his rites and the Gayatri, eats before honouring fathers, gods, men and the sun, goes without a conch, or sells or gives offered flowers, food and saffron to Shudras. The belt is again said to hold Hari at its root, Brahma in the middle, the Vedas along it and the three fires and worlds. A bhojaka who eats the sun's offered food first purifies his body, as a Brahmin does with the Purodasha cake.

01-147.json.summary: The sun tells Aruna which bhojakas he loves and which not. Dear to him are those who do not harm others' wives or goods, do not scorn the gods, wear a shaved head, anoint with oil, blow the conch, bathe and worship three times a day without anger, fast on Sunday, the sixth, the seventh and on the sun's turnings, eat one meal a day, honour fathers on their days, perform the five great sacrifices, and honour Brahmins. Enemies and unfit ones are those who trade, farm, serve kings, speak ill of the Vedas, eat Shudra food, or give offered flowers and food to Shudras and Vaishyas; he does not accept their worship. He names what he loves on the Magha seventh: oleander flowers, red sandalwood, a reader, sweet cakes, ghee, guggulu, milk baths, conch and dance, a five-coloured banner and a white umbrella. The closing verses add that a bhojaka who does his duty is to be fed and honoured, since the sun, Brahma, Vishnu and Shiva eat in his host's house, and that he is greatest among the worthy, like Kurukshetra among holy places; there is no scripture beyond the Veda and no god like the sun.

01-148.json.summary: Samba sees a blazing discus in his father Krishna's hand and asks where it came from. Krishna says he won it by worshipping the sun for a divine thousand years. He explains the discus as a wheel of time: the sun stands in it, the planets in the hub, the twelve Adityas as spokes, the elements along its paths, six seasons as a six-petalled lotus, the months as spokes, the half-months as rims, and the two turnings of the sun as the felly; stars, planets and all times are in it. He got it to kill demons. One who worships the sun in the wheel gets glow and the sun's city. Drawing the wheel on the seventh and worshipping the sun with red sandalwood, saffron, red flowers, fruit, incense, cloth, food, dance, music and chant gives wishes, protects one's own kingdom and defeats enemies; writing and reciting it at an eclipse or turning day makes the planets kind and gives long life and health.

01-149.json.summary: Krishna gives the measures and mantras of the sun-wheel and the rite of initiation. The wheel is sixty-four finger-widths round with an eight-finger rim; the hub, lotus, spokes, petals and four doors are measured and coloured (yellow ground, white hub, red rest). The centre is worshipped as Khasholka (the sun) with limbs of the body and the other gods around, using mantras ending in "namah" or "svaha", with a 24-syllable Gayatri to the sun. Initiation may be given to Brahmin, Kshatriya, Vaishya or Shudra, man or woman, by a pure and truthful teacher: on the sixth, fire is kindled, the sun worshipped, the pupil bathed and touched with the limbs of the god, given a twig to clean the teeth, and the direction in which it points marks his guardian. Dreams afterwards are read: temples, fire, rivers, flowers, a learned Brahmin or a king are good; eating meat or drinking wine in a dream also brings the earth; bad dreams need a hundred offerings. The pupil makes his family and name known by throwing a flower on the sun's disc, hears the sun's rules, worships at dawn, noon and dusk, never eats without seeing the sun, and does not step over the image's shadow, treating all times as the sun's own.

01-150.json.summary: Krishna explains how to worship the sun on a prepared ground with eight circles in a wheel of twelve spokes, with an eight-petalled lotus in the centre. The sun is worshipped in the middle with four arms, with Aruna in front, Nikshubha to the right, Raivata, Pingala and Samjna, the scribe in the south-east, the Ashvins in the south-west, Manu Vaivasvata in the north-west, and the river Yamuna in the north-east. Further rings hold the sky, Garuda, Airavata's son, Heli, Praheli, Urvashi, Vinata, the planets Jupiter, Saturn, Moon, Rahu and others, Skanda's guards, the guardians of directions with Shiva and Kubera, Mahashveta with goddesses such as Shri, Riddhi and Earth, the twelve Adityas (Indra, Vishnu, Aryaman, Bhaga, Parjanya, Vivasvan and others), the sun's weapons and chariot, seasons and months. The mantra is "om khasholkaya namah". Worship on both sevenths gives the highest place. The sun then goes home.

01-151.json.summary: Shatanika praises the sun's greatness and asks Sumantu for an easy way to be freed from rebirth through the sun, since he has heard many Vaishnava, Shaiva and Puranic duties but wants the sun's own way, and since costly sacrifices are beyond the poor. Sumantu says the sun told this long ago to Aruna, Krishna, Brahma and Shiva. Those who remember the sun even once, twice or thrice daily are freed from sin, and his devotees are not common people but those fallen from heaven. The core is firm devotion in sixteen parts: morning bath, recitation, fire offering, worship of the god, honour to Brahmins, worship of the cow and the pipal, hearing the Itihasa and Purana, study of the Vedas, kindness to people, approval of worship, personal worship with a reader before the image, care of the book, hearing his stories, constant remembrance and so on. The sun says even an outcaste devotee is to be honoured like him, and that one who offers a leaf, flower, fruit or water with love is never lost to him.

01-152.json.summary: Sumantu, in praise, says devotion, worship, gifts and fire offerings for the sun, and knowledge of him, are very hard to gain, and blessed are the feet that circle his temple, the hands that worship, the tongue that praises, and the mind that gives up sense objects. Shatanika then asks Sumantu to tell, in detail, the rewards of the many acts of sun worship: setting up the sun, building a temple, sweeping, plastering, lamp-waving, dance and music, offering water, many kinds of baths (water, five nectars, curds, honey, milk, cane juice), anointing, flowers, garlands, incense, lamps, cloth and ornaments, hearing the Purana, giving the belt, honouring the Magas, and worshipping the sky and Aruna. The chapter has only this question.

01-153.json.summary: Sumantu tells Shatanika how the three great gods were humbled. At the start of a cycle each of Brahma (creator), Vishnu (keeper) and Shiva (destroyer) grew proud and quarrelled over who alone could create, keep and end the world. Darkness and confusion covered them, and they could not see one another or anything else; Shiva called out for Krishna and Brahma, Vishnu answered that he too was lost, and Brahma said he was blind and asleep with confusion. Then an unmatched eight-horned light, a hundred yojanas wide and ringed with flames, appeared in the sky for their awakening and lit the world. Amazed, they praised it, and the thousand-rayed sun showed himself. Brahma, Shiva and Vishnu each speak a hymn naming him Vishnu, Shiva, Indra, time, the Vedas, sacrifice, and the one from whom they themselves were born. Pleased, the sun offers boons: Brahma thanks him for sight, Shiva asks for steady devotion and union with him, and Vishnu asks for devotion and strength to be unbeaten by demons, to guard beings and the classes, and the means to worship him.

01-154.json.summary: The sun grants Vishnu's wishes: he will be unbeatable and able to guard the world, Brahma able to create, Shiva able to destroy, all by his grace. Shiva asks how they can worship him, since they see only a blaze of flames with no form to rest the mind on. The sun explains he has four forms: a passionate one (Brahma, creating), a good one (Vishnu, keeping and killing demons), a dark one (Shiva, ending the world), and a fourth beyond all qualities that cannot be seen or touched without worshipping him as the sky-form "vyoma". The blaze they saw was shown to wake them from pride. At the end of an age all gods melt into this sky: Brahma at its right, Vishnu at its left, Shiva in its hair, Gayatri in its heart, the Vedas in its head. He tells Shiva to worship the vyoma for a divine thousand years on Mount Gandhamadana, Vishnu at Kalapagrama and Brahma at Pushkara, after which they will see his highest form like a ball of kadamba flowers wreathed in rays. Vishnu asks for the vyoma's marks.

01-155.json.summary: The sun describes the vyoma to Vishnu: a wonderful four-cornered form shining with red ochre, worshipped by Brahma, Vishnu and Shiva at noon. The gods, grateful for having seen him, plan to worship the vyoma. The sun tells them the blaze was meant to wake them from pride, and that they should drop ego and worship him. He vanishes; Brahma goes to Pushkara, Vishnu to Shaligrama and Shiva to Gandhamadana, each worshipping in the four-cornered vyoma with perfume, garlands, dance and song for a divine thousand years. Pleased, the sun shows himself in four forms at once. He tells Brahma to ask a boon; Brahma asks for strength to create, and the sun says he will be born in Brahma's line, so that creation succeeds; he gives Brahma a home on the sky-form's rear horn. Directions are given for gods around it: Indra east, Yama south, Nirriti, Varuna, Vayu, Kubera, Shiva in the north-east, and Brahma with Vishnu in the middle. Shiva asks to defeat all beings and end the world at the age's close; the sun grants this and makes the trident his weapon.

01-156.json.summary: Sumantu says that after giving a boon to Ishvara (Shiva), the sun went quickly to Shalagrama to give a boon to Hari (Vishnu). There he found Vishnu doing hard penance, wearing a black antelope skin and worshipping the great wheel-shaped sky with perfumes, garlands, dance and song. Vishnu bowed to the sun and praised him with a hymn: remover of poverty, disease and sorrow, lord of the planets, and the one who saves those sunk in the ocean of rebirth. The sun, pleased, offered a boon. Vishnu asked for steady devotion, the power to defeat enemies, a supreme place honoured by all worlds, and strength, fame and skill to protect the worlds. The sun granted these, saying the sky-wheel would become Vishnu's weapon (the discus). Sumantu closes by calling this the tale of the three gods (Shiva, Vishnu, Brahma) with three hymns, and promises to those who hear or recite it a son, wealth, learning, and at last the sun's highest place.

01-157.json.summary: Shatanika speaks. He is amazed that the sun, who gave Brahma a boon, was born as a son in Kashyapa's line, and asks how he came to be in a womb. He lists the sun's great works: he made the three worlds, the earth and the elements; he is the thousand-headed, thousand-eyed lord, from whose mouth, chest and brow Brahma, Hari and Shankara were born; he rides a one-wheeled chariot with Aruna as charioteer; he drives away darkness and keeps sacrifice, the seasons and the measures of time in order. A long passage describes how a body forms in the womb from the humours, the seven body substances, the five breaths and the five elements, with the sun in the middle of the body. From all this Shatanika asks again how the unborn lord entered the womb of Aditi, and asks Sumantu to tell the wonderful story and the sun's strength.

01-158.json.summary: Sumantu replies that it is a large question and promises to tell it as best he can. He first praises the sun with many "thousand" names (thousand rays, eyes, tongues, arms) and says the sun has appeared in many ages and will appear again. Then the story: the sun was born as Kashyapa's son by Aditi, but each son she bore died at once. Grieving, Aditi went to Kashyapa, who found him shining and doing penance in a hermitage, and told him her sorrow. Kashyapa went to Brahma's world; Brahma said they should go to the sun's abode, and the three (Aditi, Kashyapa, Brahma) travelled there by a fiery vehicle. They reached the sun's great hall, filled with Vedic chanting and with learned sages, and saw Daksha, Marichi, Bhrigu, Atri, Vasishtha, Narada and others waiting on the sun, along with the elements, the Vedas, the seasons and the aims of life. After the sun spoke to them, Kashyapa and Aditi returned home. Aditi carried the child for a thousand divine years, and when it was born the sun destroyed hosts of Daityas and the world rejoiced.

01-159.json.summary: Sumantu continues. Daksha and the sages bow to the newborn sun while the Gandharvas sing. The sun is named as twelve forms: Indra, Vivasvan, Pusha, Tvashta, Savita, Bhaga, Amshuman, Aryaman, Arka, Prishni, Martanda and Vishnu. The Rudras, Ashvins, eight Vasus, Garuda, the serpent king Vasuki, Aruna and others stand with folded hands. Brahma comes and says that since the sun looks on everything he shall be lord of the world and called "Vivasvan", and, being the first god, "Aditya". The chapter praises the sun as the goal of sacrificers, yogis and sages who do not return to rebirth. Kashyapa and Aditi are delighted with the glowing, honey-coloured child, who tells Kashyapa he came as his son to make his boon to Brahma true and asks him to carry on creation. Brahma gained creation and Kashyapa gained a son by worshipping the sun.

01-160.json.summary: Shatanika praises the sun and asks what form Brahma, Vishnu and the gods saw after worshipping him. Sumantu answers: Brahma and Vishnu went to the Himalaya, to Shiva, and found him worshipping the sun. They said they had come to worship the sun but had not seen his highest form, and the three went together to the Udaya mountain (the eastern mountain of sunrise) and did penance for a thousand divine years: Brahma on a lotus seat, Shiva standing with arms raised, Vishnu head down between five fires. The sun was pleased and offered them a boon. They said they already had his grace for creation, upkeep and ending, but asked to see his supreme form. He showed a wonderful form of all the gods: earth as his feet, sky as his head, fire and sun as eyes, Sarasvati as tongue, Brahma as heart, Kashyapa as belly, the Vedas and sacrifices in his chest and so on. Terrified, they fell to the ground and begged him to withdraw it. The sun, smiling, said he had shown it for their good, and then vanished. The chapter ends by saying the gods, Gandharvas and sages reached the highest success by worshipping the sun.

01-161.json.summary: A short chapter of nine verses, spoken by Shatanika. He agrees with what was said before: there is no god equal to the sun and no refuge equal to him. The three worlds have the sun as their root; everything is born from him and returns into him; gods such as Rudra, Indra and Upendra get their light from him. He is time and fire, the twelve-formed lord of beings, who lights up all moving and unmoving things. Shatanika then asks what reward comes from worshipping the sun. The answer is not in this chapter.

01-162.json.summary: Sumantu answers on the reward of setting up and serving the sun. One who installs an image of the sun gains immortality and sun-like brightness; one who hates the sun goes to hell. The reward is a crore times that of all sacrifices, penances, gifts and pilgrimages, and lifts three, or even twenty-one, family lines. Special merit comes from making a sun-image of clay or of flour, adorned with scents, flowers, fruit and lamps, with aloe, sandal and red sandal placed on the four sides, offered on the seventh of the dark half. The chapter stresses that devotion, not the size of the gift, decides the fruit: rich and poor are equal, and a rich man who gives out of stinginess or without devotion gets nothing. It advises dividing one's wealth, one third for living and two thirds for dharma. Building a sun temple of stone, brick, wood or even clay (even by a child at play) brings a place in the sun's world and later birth as a righteous king. Sweeping and plastering the temple, using filtered cow dung and water, drawing floors and painting pictures of the gods and planets all bring long stays in heaven. The chapter closes by saying that, without the sun, none can free creatures from the bonds of worldly attachment.

01-163.json.summary: Sumantu continues, on the sun's bathing and worship. At bathing time one should arrange auspicious signs, vessels, drums and conch, and Veda chanting at the three twilights, and wave lights (nirajana). He ranks the baths: the "Brahma bath" with the five cow products of a tawny cow and kusha water; ghee, milk, curds, honey, rice paste, sugar-cane juice, fruit water, sandal water and camphor-and-aloe water, each with its reward; and a combined three-bath giving the fruit of a thousand horse sacrifices. Ghee bathing is held the best and removes sins of this and past lives; a month of ghee bathing carries many family lines to the sun's temple. He then explains the eight-part offering (arghya) of water, milk, kusha tips, ghee, curds, honey, red oleander and red sandal, and says the reward grows with the vessel: clay, bamboo, copper, silver, gold, in rising order. After this come perfumes and pastes (sandal, aloe, saffron), fans, and flowers. Flowers are ranked: oleander beats a thousand ordinary flowers, with lotus, bakula, mudgara, shami leaves and blue lotus rising above it. Impure, stale or scentless flowers are to be avoided, and if flowers are not to be had, leaves, fruits, grasses or herbs may be offered, since devotion is what pleases the sun. The chapter ends with flower canopies and flower-decked houses, which bring a flower-chariot journey to the sun's city.

01-164.json.summary: Shatanika asks again for the reward of worshipping the sun, and Sumantu answers by retelling a talk of the three gods. Vishnu and Shiva ask Brahma (seated in Manovati) what merit worship of the sun brings, and Brahma replies at length. Merit comes from planting a garden of mango, bilva, jasmine, oleander, bakula, ashoka, champaka and other trees for the sun; from burning incense (guggulu with ghee, aloe, camphor), especially on the dark seventh; from offering a sacred thread, cloth, canopy, umbrella, banners, bells, drums and conches; from food offerings in rice, sweets and milk-rice, with the reward counted by the number of grains; from lamps (especially a lamp-garland in Kartika and lamps on a lamp-tree); and from a mirror, circumambulation and full-length bowing, which equals sacrifices. It also praises serving the sun's temple with music, flag-lines and a Bhaga rite, and an evening offering. Next is the Krishna-shashthi vow: a night meal on the dark sixth and seventh, with a different name of the sun in each month (Amshuman, Bhanuman, Divakara, Martanda, Vivasvan, Chandakirana, Divaspati, Arka, Aryaman, Bhaskara, Bhaga, Shakra) and a matching cow product or food taken, such as ghee, milk, cow's horn water, or dung. At the year's end Brahmins who are sun devotees are fed, and a black milch cow is given. Sumantu closes by saying the sun first told this sixth-day vow to Aruna, and that it frees from all sin.

01-165.json.summary: Sumantu tells the sun's "night-meal" vow (naktabhojana) month by month, each with a fast on the seventh of both fortnights, worship at the three twilights and sleeping on the ground. In Pausha, one eats rice, wheat and milk foods, and at month's end bathes the sun with ghee, offers milk-sweets, feeds eight Brahmins and gives a tawny (kapila) cow. In Magha one eats oil-cake with ghee, bathes the sun in ghee on the eighth and gives a dark young cow; Phalguna brings millet and milk, a bath of the five cow products and earths, and a red cow; Chaitra brings rice with milk-rice and a pale-red cow; Vaishakha, sugar-ghee food; Shravana, milk and rice with a yellow cow; Bhadrapada, leftovers of fire offering, sleeping under a tree and a red-brown cow; Ashvina, measured food and a lotus-coloured cow; Margashirsha, milk food and a red cow. Each month is paired with a different kind of heavenly chariot and a stay in the sun's city. Rules common to all: not harming, truthfulness, no stealing, patience, honesty. The chapter says these vows destroy sin and disease and give all wishes, and that the sun's way brings knowledge and, through it, freedom from rebirth.

01-166.json.summary: The chapter begins with the first verse missing in the text, and the speaker is not marked. It teaches the "Nikshubha-Arka" vow for a woman devoted to the sun who wants a good son. On the seventh, the sixth or a Sunday or sankranti, she fasts and makes a fire offering; she makes an image of Nikshubha (the sun's consort) in bronze, gold or silver and bathes it with ghee for a year; she adorns it with scents, garlands and cloth, feeds sun devotees dressed in white, and carries the image on her head, under a canopy and with banners and conches, to the sun's temple. The fruit is journeys in sun-bright chariots to the sun's world, then long stays in Vishnu's and Brahma's worlds, and later worlds of the Moon, Indra and the Gandharvas; the text also says the devoted woman will surely become a man. The chapter ends by saying that, so long as death has not come, beings wander by their deeds, and that detachment leads to knowledge, knowledge to yoga, and yoga to the end of sorrow.

01-167.json.summary: Sumantu continues the vows of the sun's consort Nikshubha, now for women. A celibate, self-controlled woman who goes without food on the sixth and seventh for a year, and makes an image called Nikshubha with the bath and other steps given earlier, rides golden four-doored chariots to the sun's city, later returns to earth and gets a king for a husband. A woman who fasts on one dark seventh and at year's end offers a rice-flour image, with yellow paste, garlands and cloth, gets seven great chariots, a long stay in the sun's world, and later a husband with all good marks, wealth and grain. Another woman, firm in her vow on the dark seventh, offers a perfumed Nikshubha-Arka image set with gold, gems and pearls, with the same fruit. Finally, a person who keeps the vow for a year feeds a married pair among the sun's bhojaka priests, honours them with scents, garlands and cloth, and gives a golden Nikshubha-Arka in a copper vessel; the text says Nikshubha is the bhojika and the sun the bhojaka, so the pair should be honoured with faith.

01-168.json.summary: Sumantu speaks of the sun vows for women and others, month by month. First a woman who eats once a day through Kartika, keeps forbearance and non-violence, and offers rice with jaggery and ghee, oleander flowers and guggulu on the seventh and sixth, gets chariots like blue sapphires, a long stay in the sun's world, and later a king as husband. Ten duties common to all vows are named: patience, truth, kindness, giving, cleanliness, control of senses, sun worship, fire offering, contentment and not stealing. Then follow monthly offerings of figures made of flour or grain, decorated and set in the sun's temple: a chariot in Magha, a sun image in Phalguna, an image of Aruna in Chaitra, a Mount Meru of rice flour with Nikshubha-Arka in Vaishakha (called the "great sky vow"), a flour lotus full of seeds in Ashadha, a mountain of sesame in Shravana, a sky of rice in Bhadrapada, and a mountain of grain with gold and cloth in Ashvina. Each gives a stay in the sun's world, return to earth, and a husband who is a king. The chapter ends by saying men, women and eunuchs alike get whatever they wish by worshipping the sun with devotion.

01-169.json.summary: Sumantu says that giving a house, hermitage or temple for the sun (of clay, wood, stone or brick, stocked with grain and goods) brings every wish. Then the chariot vow: eating once a day in the cold season and Magha, one makes a chariot with four white horses, banners, umbrellas, fans and mirrors; on it one places a sun figure of rice flour with his wife Sanjna, drives it at night through the royal road with conch and drum, spends the night awake in worship in the sun's temple, bathes the figure at dawn with honey, milk and ghee, feeds the poor, the blind and the needy, and gives the chariot to the sun. This "sun vow" is called the best of vows, giving the fruit of all vows and sacrifices, twenty-one family lines lifted, a stay in the sun's world and then rebirth as a righteous king. Another rite sets up the sun and Sanjna, made of flour, with a teacher of sun-knowledge, honours the teacher with scents, flowers, cloth, food and a bed, and counts the reward by the number of threads and wool in the bed's covers. The chapter ends with the gift of ten cows with a bull (eleven in all), which makes the giver like the twelve Adityas, with the eight powers, and a follower of the sun.

01-170.json.summary: A very short chapter that stops abruptly in the source (its sixth verse is cut off). Sumantu says that giving a hundred cows with a bull to the sun lifts twenty-one family lines; the giver goes in countless chariots to the sun's city, plays in the sun's hall, and at the end of the world drops the cloak of delusion and enters the sun's circle, becoming all-knowing, pure, established in the self, and shining like the sun. The last verse starts to say that giving a two-mouthed cow (one in the act of calving) to the sun earns the same fruit as giving the earth with its seven continents.

01-171.json.summary: Shatanika asks for the duty of the Magas (the sun's priests) and its reward. Sumantu says the sun-duty already taught is the Maga duty, and any of the four classes, or a woman, may follow it. The Maga worships the sun at the three twilights, does the fire rite with his mouth covered, and never eats without first worshipping the sun; eating before worship is called eating filth. He should not pick flowers harmfully, should cook only for gods, fire and guests and not for himself, should be sexually restrained, honest in his earning, and divide his wealth. Four kinds of sun-devotee life are named: the celibate student, the householder, the forest-dweller and the renunciant. The "eight vows" of a bhojaka are patience, non-violence, peace, contentment, truth, not stealing, celibacy and worship by deed, mind and word. Bhojakas are to be cared for as one's own body, and anything done to them is done to the sun. The chapter also praises hospitality, kind and pleasant words as the stairs to heaven, giving shelter, fanning the tired, feeding the hungry and even birds and outcastes out of mercy, and forbearance: one who does not curse or strike back when abused or struck is freed from sorrow.

01-172.json.summary: Sumantu continues on sun duty. Wherever one sees the sun being worshipped, one should go and honour him, and one who meets a bhojaka on the road should get down and honour him. The chapter says to feed bhojakas at festivals, shraddha and on holy days, because the ancestors rest in the sun and are pleased when he is; a bhojaka fed at a shraddha lifts seven family lines. Defining a bhojaka: calm, free of hate and desire, with knowledge, devoted to the sun, free of heresy. There is a ladder of worth (man, twice-born, learned, the Veda-knower, the one who knows the truth, the yogi, and above all the bhojaka), and the sun-duty is said to lead to knowledge, then detachment, then sun-union and freedom. Short definitions are given of the gift of land, a bride, cloth, fasting and the Chandrayana, and the eightfold marks of a worthy recipient. Gifts to bhojakas that are praised: a seat, cloth, a woollen blanket, a conch and sandals, and having a Purana copied. The chapter closes with how to honour a teacher who explains the sun-duty: a large decorated gooseberry (amalaka) seat for the speaker, with the teacher honoured like the sun, and long life, learning and fame for one who hears and tells it.

01-173.json.summary: Shatanika asks Sumantu again for the sun-duty, told at greater length. Sumantu praises him and retells an old talk between Garuda and Aruna (the sun's charioteer). Garuda asks Aruna for the best of duties, the sun-duty, and Aruna answers. It crosses the ocean of ignorance; those who remember, praise and worship the sun go to the highest place, and one who does not worship him has wronged himself. Human birth is rare, so those who worship the sun make it fruitful. The rewards listed are fine things, women, wealth, kingdom, good fortune, beauty, fame and a good name. Aruna notes that devotion to the sun, worship, giving, fire offering and knowledge of him are all hard to get. One who keeps the name "Ravi" on the tip of the tongue and worships with faith is freed from sin; spirits, demons and enemies cannot harm him, he wins battles and is free of disease, and wealth, long life, fame and learning grow.

01-174.json.summary: Aruna continues to Garuda. Brahma, Vishnu, Shiva and Indra each reached their rank by worshipping the sun, and everything in the world rests on him. One who does not worship him gets none of the four aims of life; it is better to give up life than to go without sun worship, and one should worship all one's life even in trouble. Devotees of the sun are described as patient, truthful, humble, kind, not proud, free of greed and attached to nothing, like a lotus leaf in water. The sun is called the best of all worthy recipients, since he saves the falling from the ocean of hell, and even a small gift to him is highly rewarded. Aruna gives the order of incense, sandal, aloe and saffron by merit, and warns that life, youth and health pass quickly, so one should worship now, before death, old age or weakness comes. The chapter ends with a hymn, spoken by Brahma, bowing to the sun by many names, with a promise of fame for one who hears it daily. (The chapter's verse numbers are slightly irregular in the source.)

01-175.json.summary: Garuda asks what those afflicted by disease, the harm of the planets, enemies or obstacle-spirits should do, and Aruna replies that nothing is better than worship of the sun. Garuda explains that a Brahmin woman's curse has stripped him of his feathers and left him ill, and that he cannot do the worship or the fire rite. Aruna says he will do the fire offering himself, as the sun once did for him: a "lakh offering" (hundred-thousand fire offerings) that gives peace, ends untimely death and disease and wins victory. He sets a sacred ground in the south-east with cow dung and gives the offering words (with "bhur bhuvah svah" and "svaha") to the deities of the directions in turn, from Brahma and Indra in the east to Yama, Varuna, Vayu, Kubera and Ishana, each described by colour and weapon. The bhojaka then does a peace rite for all the worlds, praying that the sun and the planets (the Moon, Mars, Mercury, Jupiter, Venus, Ketu and others) remove the troubles caused by the planets.

01-176.json.summary: A short chapter of eight verses, marked as spoken by Sumantu, though it reads as the continuation of the peace prayer begun in the previous chapter. It asks three gods in turn to bring peace, each described by form and each said to be devoted to the sun. First Brahma: lotus-seated, four-faced, holding a water pot, eldest of the gods, lord of creatures. Then Vishnu: dressed in yellow, dark in colour, four-armed with conch, discus and mace, called Madhava and Madhusudana. Last Shiva (Maheshvara): white like the moon, four-armed, four-faced, smeared with ash, living in cremation grounds, and born from the sun's body. (The text's verse numbers and speaker mark may be slightly off in the source.)

01-177.json.summary: Aruna continues the peace prayer to Garuda, now calling on goddesses to bring peace to the one for whom the rite is done, each said to be devoted to the sun. The seven Mothers come first: Brahmani (lotus-coloured, four-faced, with prayer beads and water pot), Maheshvari or Rudrani (white, riding a great bull, with a trident), Kaumari (peacock-riding, red, with a spear), Vaishnavi (dark, four-armed with mace and discus), Indrani (on Airavata, thunderbolt in hand), Varahi (boar-faced, with conch, discus and mace), and the fierce Chamunda (gaunt, skull-garlanded, living in the burial ground). Then the sky-mothers, world-mothers, the mothers of beings and of ancestors who are honoured at the ancestor rite for good fortune are invoked, and finally Uma, the boon-giver, with a moon-mark on her brow. All are asked to give peace and to be pleased with their bali offering.

01-178.json.summary: Aruna continues the peace prayer, asking more gods and their followers to bring peace to the one for whom the rite is done. Named are Skanda (Kartikeya) as a youth on a peacock, Nandi, the elephant-faced lord Ganesha (Vinayaka, lord of the hosts), a blue three-eyed lord (probably a form of Shiva), the goddess mother of the gods, Durga who slays the great buffalo, Bhringi, and Chandeshvara, who removes sin. Groups of fierce Rudras, Mothers and obstacle-spirits in all directions are asked to accept the offering and give success. Then comes a tour of the ruling gods of the eight directions and their cities: Indra in Amaravati (east), Agni in his city (south-east), Yama, called Antaka, in Vaivasvati (south), the demon lord in the city called Krishna (south-west), the western lord in Shuddhavati (west), and Ishana in Yashovati (north-east). Gods of the lower and upper worlds, and Sarasvati and Aparajita, are also invoked.

01-179.json.summary: Aruna ends the long peace prayer, calling on the heavenly groups, each devoted to the sun, to give peace and growth to the one for whom the rite is done. The lunar mansions (nakshatras) are named in groups by direction, east to north, from Krittika and Rohini to Bharani; then the zodiac signs (Mesha, Simha, Dhanu in the east, Vrishabha, Kanya, Makara in the south, Mithuna, Tula, Kumbha in the west), the seven sages and a list of other sages (Kashyapa, Gargya, Vishvamitra, Vasishtha, Narada, Bhrigu, Valmiki and more), and the daughters of sages. Next are Siddhas, Vidyadharas and Garuda; and daityas, including Namuchi, Prahlada, Hayagriva, Kalanemi, Vairochana and Hiranyaksha, all said to worship the sun. Then come the serpent kings, Ananta, Takshaka, Karkotaka, Padma, Shankhapala and Kulika, and the serpents of the sky, earth and the underworld, asked to remove poison. The chapter ends with a promise that one who recites or hears this list is not harmed by snakes and poison does not work on him.

01-180.json.summary: The peace prayer (spoken by Aruna to Garuda; no speaker is marked at the start) ends. It calls on rivers (Ganga, Yamuna, Narmada, Gautami, Kaveri and others), the yaksha lords (Kubera, Manibhadra, Suchira, Panchika, Dhritarashtra, Virupaksha) with their wives and children, all mountains, trees and oceans, and the rakshasas, ghosts, pishachas and the spirits that cause epilepsy and fever, all asked to bring peace through the sun's power. Hymns of "victory" to the sun follow, calling him lord of the planets, dispeller of darkness, and the one in the form of the Gayatri. At that moment Garuda's feathers grow back and he is whole again, shining and strong. The chapter then says this fire rite heals sick people too, and should be done at planetary harm, famine, bad omens or lack of rain, with a lakh offering, Vedic hymns, ghee, honey, sesame, barley and milk-rice. Those who read or hear this "peace chapter" win over enemies, are free of disease, snakes and poison and untimely death, and even those who killed a cow, a Brahmin or their parents are freed from sin. It is not to be given to fools. The teaching is traced from the sun to Aruna, to Garuda, to the bhojakas in Shakadvipa, and to Vyasa.

01-181.json.summary: Shatanika asks for the five kinds of smriti (remembered) duty, and Sumantu retells what the sun told Aruna. The sun, rising, is asked by Aruna (called Anuru here) to explain smriti-duty. The sun answers that it rests on the Veda; duty is action that leads to well-being and heaven. It is of five kinds, named by class, by stage of life, by both together, by quality (for example a king's protection of his subjects) and by occasion (for example atonement rites). When a smriti text conflicts with the Veda, the Veda wins. He then names five sorts of smriti: those with a seen purpose, an unseen purpose, a restating role, both, and one resting on reasoning, with examples: the twilight prayer, not eating dog's flesh, carrying a palasha staff. Aruna asks for the meaning of these and the sun explains. The chapter ends with the lands where duty is practised: Brahmavarta (between the Sarasvati and Drishadvati rivers), Madhyadesha (between the Himalaya and Vindhya, west of Prayaga), Aryavarta (from the eastern to the western sea) and the land where the black antelope roams, fit for sacrifice; beyond that is the land of outsiders. A Shudra who is hard up for a living may settle in any of them.

01-182.json.summary: The sun (Aditya) continues to Aruna on the duty of the stages of life and on marriage. Four stages are named (student, householder, forest-dweller, renunciant) and four kinds of celibate student. Then the life-cycle rites: conception, the male-child rite in the third month, hair-parting in the seventh, birth rite, naming, first rice-feeding in the sixth month, topknot at the first or third year, and the sacred-thread rite at eight or ten for a Brahmin and eleven or twelve for Kshatriyas and Vaishyas. Next, how a student finishes study and leaves his teacher. A man should marry a woman of his own class, outside his own family and clan, with good marks, and the text sets out a rule on girls' ages (gauri at seven, nagnika at ten, kanya at twelve, then one who has begun her period), saying a girl should be given before she reaches puberty. It lists the eight kinds of marriage (Brahma, Prajapatya, Arsha, Daiva, Gandharva, Asura, Rakshasa, Paishacha) with the lowest being forced union with a sleeping or drunk woman. The chapter also covers the marrying-order rule for brothers, whom not to marry, fines for hiding a bride's faults, how many wives each class may have (from one for a Shudra to four for a Brahmin), a wife's property, and when a man may take another wife. This is a record of old social rules and is given as the text says it.

01-183.json.summary: The chapter begins mid-teaching, with no speaker marked, and the sun (Aditya) goes on to explain to Aruna (called Anuru) the five great daily sacrifices to beings, ancestors, gods, Brahma (study) and men (hospitality). It then sets out twelve kinds of ancestor rite (shraddha), each defined: the daily (nitya), the one for a single dead person (ekoddishta, called naimittika), the wish-based (kamya), the growth-rite (vriddhi), the rite joining the dead to the ancestors (sapindana), the new-moon and festival rite (parvana), the cow-pen, the purification, the rite-part (karmanga), the divine, the journey rite and the one for bodily growth. The yearly rite on the death day is called the best, and the sun says that he, Vishnu, Brahma, Rudra and the other gods do not accept the worship of one who skips it; a sun devotee especially must keep it every year for his parents, or fall into the hell Tamisra and be born a pig. If the death day is not known, it is done on the new moon in Margashirsha or Magha. The chapter ends with the sun saying that ancestors, cows and Brahmins are dear to him and are to be honoured.

01-184.json.summary: The chapter has no speaker mark at the start; it carries on the sun's talk with Aruna (called Anuru), who speaks at verse 31, and the sun at verse 37. It gives rules on Brahmin conduct and food. Selling the Veda in six ways (taking gifts, sacrificing, teaching, debating and so on) is blamed, and a Brahmin who skips the Vaishvadeva offering and the sun rite is called no better than a low-born man.
