They go to Jayachandra, say Prithviraj took his grandfather's kingdom and half is rightly his, and Jayachandra makes them his ministers and gives them the city Mahavati. Prithviraj marries a sister of the king of Mahavati, who then builds a new city; he builds a fort and a city, and a threshold (dehali) set at the gate is said to have grown old a league away, so the village is named Dehali. After three years Jayachandra, with sixteen lakh soldiers, sends a letter demanding half the inheritance; Prithviraj, with twenty lakh, refuses and demands tax. Their enmity grows, each takes half the Aryan land, and the text says this enmity destroyed the fire lineage.

07-006.json.summary: Suta tells how Ratnabhanu raids the south, which Prithviraj (Mahiraja) protects, and takes its treasuries. Jayachandra's sixteen wives have no son; by his queen's maid he has a daughter, Samyogini, who at twelve holds a choosing-ceremony. Prithviraj, hearing of her beauty, sends his minister Chandrabhatta to set a golden statue of him in the assembly; Samyogini, bewitched by it, ignores the kings and tells her father she will marry the one whose statue it is. Jayachandra says the king may win her if he comes with his army; Prithviraj marches with a huge force and two brothers, and Jayachandra gathers sixteen lakh. The two armies meet by the Ishana river; Ratnabhanu and Lakshana lead for Jayachandra, with Pradyota, Vidyota, Bhishma and Parimala guarding them. Five days of great battle follow, with elephants, horses and foot soldiers dying in great numbers on both sides. On the sixth day Prithviraj praises Rudra, who confuses the opposing army; Prithviraj sees Samyogini, she faints, and he carries her palanquin off to Dehli. When the Kanyakubja side notices, they chase; at Sukarakshetra fierce fighting follows; Pradyota, Vidyota, Dhundhakara and Krishnakumara are killed, and Ratnabhanu and Krishnakumara kill each other. The Kanyakubja forces, hearing of Ratnabhanu's death, retreat with the fainted women; Prithviraj does last rites for his brother, and Bhishma, Parimala and Lakshana perform them for Ratnabhanu at the Ganga. Prithviraj's fame spreads, and Jayachandra and Prithviraj each hold feasts.

07-007.json.summary: Suta tells that Bhishma, a worshipper of Indra on the Ganga bank, pleases Indra with a month of austerity and asks for a divine mare, which Indra gives. Parimala, grieving for his father, worships Shiva with earthen lingas, and Shiva tests him by a snake-disease. After five months, powerless but still worshipping, he goes with his wife to Kashi to die and rests under a banyan tree at night. A snake at the root tells the Rudra-snake that he is cruel to a Shiva devotee; the Rudra-snake says the king is a fool for not giving hot oil. Parimala's wife Malana hears and pours hot oil into the hole; the king is healed, a thumb-sized self-born lingam appears, and he praises Shiva with the Mahimna hymn. Asked for a boon, he asks that Vishnu come and live in his house; the lingam gives a load of gold from itself each day. Parimala goes home to Mahavati and, after a year, to Jayachandra, who says he may come when the king meets trouble. Lakshana worships Jagannatha; in a fortnight the god asks his wish, and Lakshana asks for a divine mount that destroys enemies; the god makes the elephant Airavati from Airavata's power and gives her. Talana and others come to Mahavati, make friends and return; Talana gives Varanasi to his sons, who are named in a list, and he worships a demon-like god with Mleccha rites. Desharaja and Vatsaraja, by worshipping Indra and the Sun, are given a mare, an elephant named Panchashabda and a horse named Papihaka. The three heroes live at Mahavati, honoured, with sixty thousand soldiers, Talana as their lord, and the two brothers as ministers of the moon-line king.

07-008.json.summary: Suta tells that King Jambuka, with his son Kaliya, worships Shiva with earthen lingas on the Narmada bank; after six months Shiva gives him a boon that no king can defeat him. Kaliya, who also gains Shiva's boon, asks leave to go to the Ganga with an army; his sister asks him for a jewelled necklace. He bathes in the Ganga, gives gifts, and goes to Jayachandra's city, but does not get the costly necklace there. Urged by the king of Aurvi city, he goes to Mahavati with Shiva's boon and besieges it. The frightened king takes refuge in Shiva and by his order marches out with sixty thousand soldiers and three heroes, Desharaja with a thousand elephants, Vatsaraja with sixteen thousand horses, and Talana with the foot soldiers. They fight a day and a night and break the enemy army, and the people of Mahishmati flee. Kaliya rallies, takes up a stupefying arrow by Shiva's boon and stuns the three heroes; the surviving enemies strike the sleepers on the skull. Bhishmasimha wakes the soldiers with a Sun-given arrow and strikes Kaliya with a Bhairava spear, but Kaliya recovers, and cuts off Bhishmasimha's head. Talana and the others defeat Kaliya and hold the enemy back; the king, remembering Shankara, confuses his foes and returns home with half his army. Jayachandra hears of it, is amazed, and makes Talana his army chief. Five months after Bhishmasimha's death, his wife Madalasa, a Gurjara king's daughter, bears a son, a part of Sahadeva, named Devasimha by astrologers.

07-009.json.summary: Suta tells that after defeating Kaliya, the two brothers Desharaja and Vatsaraja go to the Gopalaka land, where King Dalavahana holds a thousand-Chandika fire rite attended by many kings. They seize two buffaloes no other king could master; by Durga's order the king gives them his daughters, Devaki to Desharaja and Brahmi to his younger brother, with a singer, elephants, horses, chariots, palanquins and servants. Malana gives the brides a necklace and ornaments, and Desharaja gets the city Dashapura. Devaki bears a fair, lotus-eyed son, a part of Rama, who is named Ahlada; a month later Brahmi bears Balakhani, a part of Dharmaja. A son called Chamunda is born at an unlucky star-time, and Brahmins call him a danger to his family. Madalasa's husband's brother Vatsaraja goes to the Gurjara land; meanwhile Jambuka with seven lakh soldiers besieges Mahavati, defeats the brothers by Shiva's boon, plunders and burns it, taking the courtesan, the necklace and jewels. Devaki, pregnant, throws Chamunda, who she thinks will harm the family, into the Kalindi river, and Mahiraja's priest Samanta takes him in. At ten months, on a dark night in Bhadra, Devaki bears a dark, lotus-eyed son shining like a thousand sky-chariots; a voice from the sky says he is part of Krishna, named Udayasimha. Malana bears a dark son, a part of Phalguna, and Brahmi bears a strong son named Sukhakhani. The boys grow; at three Krishna's part plays in the sandal forest and laughs at Indra in the sky, and at five they study under the Brahmin Shivasharma, with Krishna's part best in writing at eight.

07-010.json.summary: Suta says that at nine Udayasimha (Krishna's part) learns logic, the sixty-four arts and law. Prithviraj (Mahiraja) sends a lakh soldiers to Mahavati to demand a sixth of its wealth as tribute; Parimala pays, they carry off ten lakh in goods, and Mahiraja drops the old enmity. When they ask Jayachandra's son Lakshana for tribute, he takes up a Vaishnava weapon and they flee. A wrestler, Abhaya, son of the king of Aurvi, challenges the boy to a wrestling bout; the boy throws him and breaks his arms, then throws the other wrestlers one by one, and Parimala has Abhaya healed. The text explains the boy's strength by an astrologer's statement. At nine the boys ask for horses to hunt, and Parimala gives them four, which the sages ask about: Desharaja once served the Sun twelve years and received the sky-going horse Papihaka, who mated with the divine mare Harini and sired Manoratha, Karala, Bindula and Harinagara, which go to Devasimha, Ahlada, Udayasimha and Brahmananda. On the hunt they kill a tiger, a lion, a boar and a deer, then the goddess Sharada, as a golden deer, tests them; Udayasimha's arrow wounds her, and she says to remember her in fear and she will help. The king is glad and good fortune enters every house.

07-011.json.summary: Suta says that at ten the boys keep a spring vow in a pleasure garden, bathe at dawn, worship Ambika, recite the Saptashati and live on roots and fruit, and after a month the goddess gives boons: divinity to Ahlada, strength to Balakhani, knowledge of time to Devasimha, knowledge of Brahman to Brahmananda and yoga to Udayasimha. Malana bears a dark son, part of Satyaki. In Ashadha Udayasimha rides alone to Aurvi, bows to his uncle, and soldiers ordered to bind him are overcome; he kills five hundred, breaks the pots of women at a well, and defeats and binds his enemies, but spares them when they plead, and Parimala rejoices. At eleven, Prithviraj, in fear, gives tribute to his sister in Dehli, and her husband Dhundhakara raises a seven lakh army against Mahavati. Balakhani offers to defeat them, and a great battle follows in which Parimala's side loses sixty thousand and Mahiraja's half. The five young heroes kill two lakh Kshatriyas, but Dhundhakara hurts Ahlada, and Prithviraj, with Shiva's boon, strikes Balakhani and others down with a Rudra weapon. Sukhakhani, flying on his horse, makes Prithviraj faint, but he wakes and faints them again, until Udayasimha, flying, destroys the cannons and binds Prithviraj. Prithviraj, ashamed, pays five crore and goes home, and Balakhani builds Shirisha city with the wealth, which Parimala visits gladly.

07-012.json.summary: Suta says that at twelve Udayasimha (Krishna's part) is the centre of events. At a gathering of kings at Kanyakubja on the tenth of Ashvin's bright half, Lakshana wants to see him, but Jayachandra will not allow it; other kings go to Shirisha and praise him. An angry king tells them that his parents were killed at Mahishmati by Jambuka, who crushed their bodies on stones and hung their heads on a banyan tree, where they still cry out as ghosts. Udayasimha tells his weeping mother and, praising the goddess, is helped by her, who confuses Talana and sends him over. The heroes take command (Talana overall, Devasimha chariots, Balakhani horses, Ahlada elephants, Udayasimha foot soldiers), go south disguised as wandering singers and dancers, charm Mahishmati, and win the secret of Jambuka's defence from his daughter Vijayaishini, who loves Udayasimha. In a long war they bind Kaliya, Suryavarma and Tundila and kill Rankana and Vankana, but Jambuka's daughter, using illusion, carries off five heroes, and her teacher, the siddha Ailavili, who had been a demon before, is killed. Jambuka, by Shiva's boon, binds the heroes and begins a sacrifice; Devaki worships the goddess, who promises to confuse him, and the heroes break free and bind Jambuka. The three enemy sons are killed, and Udayasimha puts his parents' heads on Jambuka's heart, and a voice from the dead bodies tells him to perform the rite at Gaya. Devaki has Jambuka crushed on a stone mill, and the queen dies; her daughter wounds Balakhani and kills some heroes, and a voice tells Balakhani never to kill a woman. The army carries off the wealth to Mahavati.

07-013.json.summary: The sages ask how long the war lasted and what followed; Suta says the fighting began in Pausha and lasted a hundred days, and the heroes came home in Jyeshtha with great rejoicing, and Parimala gave gifts to Brahmins. Prithviraj [Mahiraja] then comes to Balakhani, offers him half a crore of wealth every year and asks for the Mahishmati land, and Balakhani goes home. At thirteen Udayasimha (Krishna's part) and his three companions go with Ahlada to Gaya, perform the sixteen shraddhas and give elephants, chariots, horses, cows and gold. Netrasimha, a hill king who had pleased Indra, was given the drum "Dhakkamrita" made by Parvati, whose sound revives an army, and he built the fortress Netrasimhagadha. His daughter Svarnavati, a part of Revati and helped by Kamakshi, meets Ahlada at a gathering; both faint, and Udayasimha rebukes his brother for delusion. Svarnavati sends Ahlada a letter through a parrot, saying her father has a boon from Indra and must be killed before she can marry. Ahlada marches with seven lakh men; Rupana carries his demand to Netrasimha, kills guards, and a fierce seven-day war follows in which the drum keeps reviving the enemy until Udayasimha, on Svarnavati's advice, steals the drum disguised as a garland-maker's wife. Netrasimha offers himself to Indra, who tells him that Ahlada and Udayasimha are partial incarnations and that Svarnavati should be given to Ahlada. An uncle of Ahlada, a king who calls Ahlada's family low Abhiras, urges Netrasimha to trick and kill the heroes at the wedding; Netrasimha tries this, but the heroes fight with the king's men at the marriage rounds and bind five kings. Harananda, his brother, frees them with illusion and binds Ahlada; Svarnavati, by prayer to the goddess, revives everyone and the heroes free him and return home by way of Ayodhya and the sea, with Malana holding a great festival.

07-014.json.summary: Suta says that when Udayasimha (Krishna's part) was fourteen, Jayanta, Indra's son, who had been cursed by Janaki and so had to be born in the Kali age, was born as Svarnavati's son on the ninth of Chaitra's bright half, a Thursday, with the marks of a king. The gods and sages say "this moon has come to earth", so he is named Indula. Ahlada performs the birth rites and gives gold, cows, horses and elephants to Brahmins. Two months later Yogasimha visits and gives wealth, Malana asks after the family, and a hundred dancers perform. When the child is six months old, Indra, moved by love, takes him away by his own illusion and gives him to Indrani, who nurses him so that he grows to sixteen years in appearance; he learns his father's knowledge and is named Indula because he takes in the moon's nectar. Svarnavati weeps, and ten villages mourn; Ahlada fasts with his family and takes refuge with Sharada for three nights. A voice from the sky tells him not to grieve: Jayanta has gone to heaven, will learn divine knowledge and return in three years, and will stay on earth as long as Ahlada does, after which he will take his place as Jayanta. They are consoled and live in Dashagrama, intent on knowledge.

07-015.json.summary: Suta says that after Indula goes to heaven, the heroes, grieving, worship Sharada, reciting the Saptashati three times a day for seven days. A Brahmin's son Chamunda, from a vassal's house, worships Chandika from eight years old; at twelve, as he recites the three episodes, the goddess appears to test her devotees. She says she will fill a small bowl and they should try to fill it by mental means. Sukhakhani fills it with honey, flowers and fruit, Balakhani with meat, Mulasharma with red things, and Devaki with offerings and sandalwood, but it is not filled; Ahlada offers all his limbs and Udayasimha his head, and the bowl is full. The goddess then tells Sukhakhani he will be dear to the gods, Balakhani will die after a long time, Mulasharma will become Raktabija, Devaki will go to her own world for a long time, and one of Ahlada and Udayasimha will be like a god and the other stronger. Devasimha, free of desire, will gain liberation at death. She vanishes and all are content.

07-016.json.summary: Suta says that at seventeen Udayasimha (Krishna's part) saw the following. After Ratnabhana died, Gajasena, king of Marudhanva, afraid of Prithviraj, pleased the fire god by twelve years of worship, and received a fire horse, two sons and a daughter, Gajamukti, who was told by Durga that Dharma's part [Balakhani] would choose her. At her svayamvara on the eighth of Margashirsha's bright half she garlands Balakhani; Tarak and other kings attack, Balakhani kills a hundred of them, and Tarak's sword breaks on him, and Mahiraja's eldest son carries Tarak off. Balakhani takes her away, but Gajasena, at Mahiraja's order, puts him into sleep by illusion (Durga's curse is mentioned), chains him and has outcastes beat him in an iron fort; he wakes, kills five hundred of them with blows of his palm, and Gajasena then says it is a family custom for the bridegroom first to suffer blows, offers poisoned food, which does not harm him, and binds and beats him again until his son Suryadyuti throws him into a pit. Gajamukti secretly frees him; Ahlada arrives with seven lakh men; Gajasena's fire horse burns Talana's army, Kantamala takes away the power of Krishna's part and turns the army to fire, and Ahlada prays to Durga. Indula comes from heaven on a horse whose body gives clouds that put out the fire, and the horse's saliva revives the dead. Gajasena flees, Talana binds him and his sons, Balakhani is freed, and Gajamukti's order leads to their release for the wedding; Gajasena then shuts them in an iron fort at night, where Krishna's part kills ten thousand, and at last the king washes away his sin by giving the girl and wealth. Ahlada brings home sixteen camel-loads of gold, Svarnavati joyfully embraces Indula, and Parimala has music played and gives gifts.

07-017.json.summary: Suta says that at eighteen Udayasimha was involved in this. After a grief of Mahiraja, a voice answers his Lakshachandi rite that he will have seven sons, one each year, parts of the Kauravas, and a daughter, part of Draupadi; sons Tarak (Karna's part), Nrihari, Saradana, Mardana, Suryakarma, Bhima and Vardhana are born, and a daughter Vela, with earthquakes, a goddess's laugh and a rain of blood at her birth. At twelve Vela says her husband will be the one who bathes her at the mandapa in streams of blood and gives Draupadi's ornaments. Her father writes a verse on a gold leaf, and Tarak carries it to kings; none accept, and an uncle tells him Brahmananda [Udayasimha] with Ahlada and the others is the one, so Tarak is bound, Krishna's part takes the verse and agrees to marry Vela to Brahmananda. On the thirteenth of Magha's bright half the armies come to Mahavati; Indula brings divine ornaments from Kubera through Indra, and Ahlada gives them to Vela. At each of the seven rounds of the wedding a Kaurava-part son fights a hero, hundreds of kings and Gajasena's men arrive, Mahiraja himself enters on an elephant and seizes Lakshana by Shiva's help, but Lakshana is freed and the heroes bathe Vela in the blood of a hundred kings. After a feast the men attack again and are defeated; Mahiraja complains to Parimala, and Vela weeps, and Krishna's part brings Lakshana back and threatens him. After ten days Mahiraja, weeping, asks Parimala to leave Vela, as she is only twelve, until she is ready to join her husband, and when he embraces Parimala, Parimala's bones are crushed, and Ahlada's touch does the same to Mahiraja; fire-god physicians heal both. Malana holds a festival; Lakshana makes an obscure farewell speech about two yogis, and the kings go home.

07-018.json.summary: Suta says that at twenty Indula was reciting the Saptashati beside the Sagara lake when swans from the sky praise him and say that Padmini, daughter of Aryasimha of Simhala island, with seven companions, is a fit wife for him. He flies on the swan-king to the goddess's temple at Nalini lake, where Padmini sees him, calls him and lives with him for a year in play. The goddess vanishes because Ahlada had become proud of his devotion; Ahlada is told that Lanka's rakshasas have taken Indula, and the family laments. Krishna's part promises to bring him back; the heroes march with seven lakh men, take tribute from kings on the way, bind proud ones, worship Rameshvara at Setubandha, and reach Simhala in six months. Balakhani sends Aryasimha a letter demanding his grandsons and warning him to attack Lanka, or else suffer defeat; Aryasimha, protected by Indula, fights, and Indula, with a pillar-mantra on his arrow, freezes the army. A son, Sukhasharma, fights by day and Indula with the sons of a hundred Kshatriyas by night, for six months, and Balakhani's army is gradually worn down. The chapter ends in the middle of this war.

07-019.json.summary: Suta says that Balakhani, seeing his army fall, loses heart and consults Devasimha, who knows the three times. Devasimha says that an unseen son of Indra holds their army back by day with divine weapons and destroys it by night, and that Balakhani, Talana and Krishna's part must go and defeat him. At twenty-one Udayasimha camps part of the army at the ships and takes the other half south, breaks the gate, kills the guards, loots the city and finds Padmini in the inner palace with her seven companions; he carries her off in a palanquin to camp. Balakhani and Talana destroy the enemy army, Sukhavarman is killed, and Indula revives him. Indula returns, finds his wife gone, laments and rides out alone at night; Balakhani, seeing Padmini, laments that she is fit for Indula. Indula fights: he wounds Talana, kills him with a death weapon, and uses fire, wind, Gandharva and water weapons against Krishna's part, who swallows each by yoga; then they fight with swords while gods watch. At dawn Balakhani sees a young man in matted hair and a deerskin, who swears to kill Krishna's part or else dishonour his mother Svarnavati; Balakhani drops his weapon and tells him kindly who they are. Indula learns that they are his kin, falls at his uncle's feet, says that women cloud men's minds, and asks pardon; he revives the army and Talana. Aryasimha gives Padmini to Indula with gifts of horses and elephants, and they return, celebrating at Kirtisagara and Dasharhara city. Last, Padmini is said to have been an apsara cursed by Durvasa, who lived on earth twelve years and died of consumption.

07-020.json.summary: Suta tells of Balavardhana, king of Panchala of the Bisena line, and his wife Jaladevi, who worship Varuna; their sons are Lahara and Mayuradhvaja. At twelve Mayuradhvaja, by his elder brother's order, worships Skanda for five years as a silent forest-dweller, praises him in a hymn, and asks for strength and help; Skanda grants it and he builds Mayuranagara. Lahara worships Varuna for twelve years, praises him in a hymn on the meaning of his names, and Varuna builds the city Laharinagara for him; Lahara gets a queen, Ravi, sixteen sons, parts of Dhritarashtra's sons, and a daughter Madanamanjari. At her twelve years he sends his eldest son to Mahavati to seek Devasimha as groom; Devasimha refuses marriage, keeping celibacy, and Parimala names Sukhakhani instead. A crafty king, whom the text does not name, tells Lahara that this match is unfit, that the groom is of the fire-born family and a Shudra and would mix classes, and urges him to imprison the bridegroom. Lahara raises four lakh men with his sixteen sons, and Balakhani comes on the tenth of Magha with four lakh to Laharinagara; after five days of battle the enemy is broken, Krishna's part binds the sixteen sons, and Lahara floods the army with water, but Jayanta dries it with a wind weapon. Varuna himself then has Lahara's daughter married, Lahara honours the heroes with wealth for a month, and Sukhakhani's bride is taken home by palanquin.

07-021.json.summary: The sages ask what the heroes did on returning; Suta says Parimala, hearing that horses were lost, sends Krishna's part with Devasimha and gold-laden camels to Sindhu to buy five lakh horses. They reach Mayuranagara, where in a spring garden Krishna's part meets Pushpa, a garland-maker's daughter, who tells him of Pushpavati, the king's daughter, whom the gods wanted but fear Makaranda, her brother, born of fire to Mayuradhvaja and given a stone horse by Dharma. Krishna's part is taken with love; Devasimha calms him with Sankhya verses, and after buying horses he comes home pining, and praises the goddess; Sharada gives him dreams. At twenty-three he returns to Mayuranagara and lodges in Pushpa's house, where he makes a garland that Pushpa takes to Pushpavati, who says her dreams show a man like it, and Pushpa says her sister Krishna of Mahavati made it. Krishna's part pierces his nose, takes a woman's form and goes with Pushpa to the princess, who confides her dream of a man named Udaya and promises Krishna rewards at her wedding. At the fort gate Makaranda tries to seize Krishna, who gives him heartache and flies away; Makaranda tells Pushpavati, prepares three lakh men, and in battle defeats and binds Balakhani, Ahlada and the others with his stone horse and mace. Brahmananda and Indula come with a lakh men and a letter asking for Pushpavati; after a day of battle Indula's Vaishnava weapon burns the stone horse, a Brahma weapon fells the mace, and Makaranda is bound by a serpent noose. Pushpavati is married to Krishna's part, the army revives, and Mayuradhvaja gives wealth and the heroes return to Mahavati.

07-022.json.summary: Krishna's part (Udayasimha) comes to Mahavati and Parimala holds a festival; he lives in pleasure with Pushpavati, his wife, and one day she asks who he was in a past life. He says that he was King Chandradasa, who worshipped the shaligrama stone daily and became an emperor, and that at death he set his mind on it and won union with Hari; Vishnu, asked by Kali, sent him out of his body to be born on earth. He teaches the rule of the ages as the text gives it: in the Satya age worship is by mind, in Treta by fire, sacrifice and gifts, in Dvapara by images, and in Kali by worship of Brahman; the shaligrama is Brahman itself, pleasing gods, sages and ancestors, to be worshipped with sandal by the three twice-born classes, by Shudras with bathing and devotion, and honoured by mere sight even by mlecchas. Pushpavati then tells that she was a courtesan Chandrakanti who danced before the god, then Usha, daughter of Bana, wed to Aniruddha, and now Jambuka's daughter Vijayaishini [as in the earlier war], and that by this wrong done to her her brother is to suffer. At Holi, Malana, grieving for her daughter Chandravali, weeps in a dream-sorrow; Udayasimha rides alone with ten thousand men and wealth to Chandravali's house at Balithatha, ruled by the Yadava Virasena, whose eight sons include Kamasena, Chandravali's husband. After a sad meeting with his sister, he is slandered by a crafty king as a thief, Virasena orders Kamasena to bind him, Kamasena gives poison and beats his wife, and in the fight Udayasimha kills a lakh men, but Virasena's solar weapon strikes him and his horse down, and he is bound. Parimala sends Brahmananda with a lakh men; Virasena readies the solar weapon, but Brahmananda stops it with a Brahma weapon, and the frightened king frees Udayasimha and gives his son and Chandravali, and they return with eighty thousand men to Mahavati, where Malana weeps for joy.

07-023.json.summary: Suta says that at twenty-four Udayasimha holds a feast on the tenth of Ashvin and goes at Kartik with Indula, Devasimha and ten thousand men to Barhishmati, where Chitrarekha, daughter of the Bahlika king Abhinandana and a worshipper of Chitragupta, makes a magic vehicle in the Ganga. Chitrarekha, who has enjoyed Indula in a dream, turns him into a parrot by illusion and carries him off, and Udayasimha and Devasimha, deluded, cannot find him. A wicked king, whom the text does not name, tells Ahlada falsely that Udayasimha killed Indula, and Ahlada beats him; his mother, wife and sister plead in vain, and Ahlada orders outcastes to kill him and his wife and blind them; Devasimha pays the men, takes the couple to Gajamukti, and the outcastes bring deer eyes instead. Devasimha, rebuking Ahlada, goes to seek the boy; at Mayuranagara Makaranda shelters the couple, and Dharma, pleased by his worship, tells him of Chitrarekha, her friend Kesarini and her teacher Kutuka, who spread illusion over a hundred yojanas, and gives devices. In Phalguna Udayasimha, Makaranda and Suryavarma go as singing and dancing yogis, take Suryavarma on loan from King Gajapati, and charm Bahlika's court; Chitrarekha's illusion fails, and she gives back Indula as a man and marries him. Devasimha takes Indula's letter to Ahlada, who is relieved and beats the false king; Parimala threatens him. Kings gather for the wedding; Bahlika's seven sons (Mahananda and others) and his illusionists Kutuka and Kesarini turn Balakhani's army to stone and bind eight heroes. Svarnavati and Pushpavati, in hawk form, with Makaranda and Udayasimha, cut the illusion, Pushpavati kills Kesarini and Svarnavati kills Kutuka, and the heroes are freed. Chitrarekha tries illusion again and the heroes flee, but Udayasimha returns on the eighth, revives the army, binds Bahlika, and Jayanta weds Chitrarekha, with Bahlika giving wealth, and they return in Shravana.

07-024.json.summary: Suta says that after Indula's wedding Prithviraj [Mahiraja] sadly goes to Dehli, where Tarak reports the events; the minister Chandrabhatta says he has worshipped the Vaishnavi goddess, gained knowledge and written a vernacular poem on Krishna's part. Proud of his divine horse, Prithviraj says he will take Udayasimha's four divine horses [of water, land and sky] and sends Kundanamala to ask that they be given for his daughter Vela, or else Vela's fire will destroy them. Parimala orders Ahlada to give up the horses, but Ahlada refuses, saying their lives and the horses are one; Parimala swears a terrible oath that, if they stay in his land, he will count food as Brahmin flesh, water as cow's blood, his bed as his mother's and his assembly as the sin of killing a Brahmin, and Devaki weeps. At twenty-five, on the fourteenth of Bhadra's bright half, the heroes with their wives leave for Kanyakubja, where Jayachandra, on Parimala's order, refuses them an income; Udayasimha loots the city, and Lakshana's arrow is made useless by his Vishnu mantra, so Lakshana honours him and brings peace. Jayachandra tests Ahlada and Udayasimha with two elephants, who are killed, and gives them a village. Lakshana then goes to conquer in all directions with Talana and seven lakh men: Varanasi (Rudravarman), Magadha, Anga and Vanga (Kalivarman), Ushtra (Dhoyika), Pundra (Nagapati), each paying tribute that is sent to Jayachandra. They bow to Parashurama at Mahendra mountain, return to Netrapala, and move on to Virasimhapura on Himatunga, guarded by the yogi Gorakha, who revives the fallen each evening. Devasimha says they must overcome Gorakha by dance; disguised as yogis they play music, Gorakha offers a boon, they ask for the life-giving knowledge for Ahlada, and he grants it for one year and then leaves the world for Bhartrihari. Lakshana makes the two kings his servants, conquers Kosala, and holds a Holi festival at Naimisharanya, where Suta and the sages were in meditation. Then comes the story of Balakhani's death: Prithviraj asks a vassal for his son Chamunda, who has become Raktabija by Sharada's boon, and sends him with seven lakh men against Shirisha. Balakhani and Sukhakhani fight; Raktabija's drops of blood make new warriors, but Sukhakhani's fire arrow burns them, and Balakhani binds Chamunda and sends him home dressed as a woman. Prithviraj, angry, is advised by Parimala to use a trick, and female messengers posing as Brahmin women learn that the fire arrow is what keeps the brothers alive; Prithviraj worships Shiva for a thousand days. The chapter breaks off at this point.

07-025.json.summary: Suta says that at twenty-six Udayasimha saw this. Sharadananda, a Vishvaksena-line king nicknamed Kamapala, lives at Bindugadha by Bindusara lake and prays to Prajapati; his daughter Padmini is born, and his son Padmakara follows Prithviraj [Mahiraja]. At her svayamvara kings come; Lakshana comes with Ahlada and four heroes, and Padmini garlands Lakshana, described as dark, in his prime and marked with signs of a king. Prithviraj and the kings surround him, but Talana, Ahlada, Udayasimha, Devasimha and Lakshana overcome them in a day's fight, and Prithviraj retires; Sharadananda holds the wedding and gives his daughter with wealth. Padmakara then says to Prithviraj's side that Lakshana and Ahlada's heroes, sons of Abhira mothers, are of mixed class and should be shunned, and by illusion he binds them in a stone prison. Devasimha escapes by the goddess's boon, fetches Indula from Kanyakubja, and Indula burns the illusion with a weapon of desire; the heroes break out and kill five thousand Kshatriyas, and Sharadananda gives his daughter again, with gifts. Lakshana returns home on the eighth of Magha, and Jayachandra gives a hundred villages. Prithviraj, having a boon from Shiva won by worshipping earthen lingas, marches in Phalguna with seven lakh men on Shirisha, and Chamunda besieges it. Sukhakhani kills ten thousand with a fire weapon, but Prithviraj's Rudra weapon makes a great fire in which Sukhakhani is lost. Balakhani, grieving, fights on; Prithviraj promises him half his kingdom if he crosses twelve guarded pits, and he does, killing hundreds, but the thirteenth pit is hidden under grass and earth and set with poisoned spears; his horse's foot is broken, and Chamunda cuts off his head. His wife Gajamukti burns herself with his body, Brahmananda burns Sukhakhani's body, and Prithviraj burns the empty city and goes to Dehli.

07-026.json.summary: Suta says that in Shravana Prithviraj goes to Dehli for a snake festival, and a crafty king [Mahipati] tells him to see the Vamana festival at Mahavati, then goes to Parimala and falsely warns that Prithviraj will seize Chandravali and Brahmananda by force and should be beaten by trick. Parimala attacks at night with four lakh men and kills five thousand sleeping Kshatriyas; Prithviraj wakes and fights, and Malana prays to Sharada, who tells her that her trouble will end and, appearing to Udayasimha, says his mother is being hurt. Udayasimha, Devasimha and Lakshana go under the pretext of conquest, Talana with seven lakh men, and Ahlada stays; at Kalpakshetra they become yogis, fight seven days, and Parimala's side is beaten. Prithviraj's sons (Nrihari, Mardana, Saradana, Tarak and others) and his ally Chamunda fight Parimala's sons and heroes in pairs; Parimala's side fares badly, and Prithviraj goes to the pleasure garden with sixty lakh. The heroes who went to Shirisha find it a desert, and the sage Himada tells them that Balakhani was killed by trick and shows his pyre. Udayasimha laments; Balakhani, as a ghost with his wife, tells what happened, then rises to heaven in a divine vehicle, and his part joins Yudhishthira. At Mahavati, in yogi dress, they play and dance, and Udayasimha tells Malana that the women should take the barley to the sea while they guard them. At Kirtisagara a fight follows: Abhaya is killed by Nrihari, Saradana kills Madana, Ranajit kills Nrihari and Mardana, Saradana strikes Ranajit's chest, and Tarak kills Ranajit with a poison-washed arrow. Brahmananda, grieving, takes the women home and shuts the gates; Prithviraj, grieving for his sons, vows to destroy Mahavati as he did Shirisha, calls Dhundhukara with five lakh men, and after seven days marches with eight lakh and Tarak. The chapter ends here.

07-027.json.summary: Suta says that at twenty-seven, on the tenth of Bhadra's dark half, the grieving Malana tells Jananayaka, a man of Kachchha and Gautama's line, to ride Harinagara to Kanyakubja and call her sons Ahlada and Udayasimha. He answers that they will not come because of Parimala's own words, and she faints and wants to die; Parimala's son consoles her and goes himself. The sages ask who Jananayaka is, and Suta tells that Pradyota, minister of Anangapala of Indraprastha, had a daughter Parimala [a girl of that name] who married Kamalapati, son of the king of Kachchha, and their son Jananayaka conquered kings on the Sindhu bank and held his father's land. Mahiraja came for tribute and beat him after a month; he left his land and came to Mahavati, where Parimala gave him a village. Mahiraja, urged by the crafty king, sends Chamunda to bind him; at the Netravati river Jananayaka kills a hundred men and takes the crown of the commander, and Chamunda asks for it back as a Brahmin's due. At Kutharanagara he sleeps under a banyan, and king Vamana steals his horse Harinagara; Jananayaka threatens that Udayasimha will destroy his city, and Vamana returns the horse but keeps the golden whip. At Kanyakubja he tells Lakshana that Mahiraja means to destroy the lunar line; Jayachandra, angry that Parimala abandoned him for his enemy, asks for the price of the maintenance he gave, and Udayasimha replies that his conquests repay it more than enough. Jayachandra gives seven lakh men; Vamana returns the whip; at the Vetravati river Chamunda, as Raktabija, multiplies into a thousand men and drives the heroes to Brahmananda. Parimala weeps before Ahlada, Devaki says they were cast off, and he pleads for pardon, and is made chief minister with an army; after a month of battle Udayasimha prays to Sharada, who burns Raktabija through his sword. Prithviraj, afraid, begs Parimala's pardon and vows to end the quarrel; Parimala tells him to take refuge with Lakshana, and he falls before him; in Chaitra Udayasimha performs the Gaya rite for Balakhani and feeds a thousand Brahmins.

07-028.json.summary: Suta says that at twenty-eight Udayasimha goes with Svarnavati and ten thousand men to the holy Utpalaranya on the Ganga to leave off his wedding crown, giving a thousand cows to Brahmins. Shobha, a courtesan of mleccha birth, sees him, faints, and he asks Brahmins who made the eighteen Puranas. They answer: the six of sattva (Vishnu by Parashara, Skanda by Shiva, Padma, Bhagavata by Shuka, Brahma, Garuda), six of rajas (Markandeya, Varaha, Agni, Linga, Brahmanda and Bhavishya, the last made by Mahadeva), and six of tamas (Matsya, Kurma, Narasimha, Vamana, Shiva, Vayu) [the lists as given are partly mixed]; the Bhagavata is called best, and in the Kali age King Vikrama had the sages tell the Puranas through Suta. Udayasimha hears the Bhagavata for seven days and gives gifts. Shobha, disguised as a beggar, uses magic, which Svarnavati cuts, but she steals Svarnavati's ornament and goes to Bahlika; Svarnavati gives him a pill for protection. At Shukarakshetra Shobha deceives him by a tale of her dead brother and troupe, takes the pill, turns him into a parrot and carries him to Sarattanagara, where at night she turns him back into a man and embraces him. Udayasimha praises the goddess, and when she presses him, he answers that a man who goes to a woman not his wife goes to hell, that the sages' deeds cannot be copied, and teaches that the Vedic words come from the Brahma's mouths, and that one should never speak Yavani speech or enter a Jain temple. Angry, Shobha beats him, keeps him a parrot and feeds him only fruit; Svarnavati comes as a hawk, turns him into a mosquito and takes him to Mayuranagara, where Makaranda shelters her. Shobha, finding him gone, goes to the spirit Mahamada, who is sent by Shiva to help; with five thousand actors they march on Mayuranagara, and Indula and Ahlada come with three lakh men and Devasimha. Shobha creates a terrible storm and a spell of love, which Makaranda burns and Svarnavati breaks; Mahamada makes beasts and Svarnavati makes Sharabhas that eat them; Shobha becomes Svarnavati's servant, and the heroes go home in Vaishakha after four months of war.

07-029.json.summary: The sages ask where the girl Kinnari came from, and Suta tells that in the Chaitraratha forest in spring the apsara Manjughosha came to the sage Shuka's place, sang and danced, and praised him; he offered a boon, she asked him to be her husband, and they had a son, Muni, who practised austerity for twelve years. Kubera and Rudra gave Muni a wife, the daughter of Svarnadeva; their daughter Kinnari, born on Himatunga, practised austerity, and Shankara gave her to Makaranda. The sage asked Shiva for a lasting kingdom for her, and Shiva said it would be happy in the middle country for thirty years and then perish. Suta then tells that at twenty-nine Bauddhasimha, a Buddhist king, thinking Netrapala's city weakly ruled, besieged it with seven lakh men; after a week of battle Yogasimha, Bhogasimha and Vijaya beat the army, but Buddhist illusionists from Shyama and Japaka lands came and the fighting went on for a month. Udayasimha, Devasimha, Indula, Gautama, Talana, Dhanyapala (an oil-presser, part of Yuyutsu) and Lallasimha (a betel-seller, part of Kuntibhoja) came at Netrapala's call, and the Buddhists fled to China and returned in Magha with Chinese forces, ten lakh strong; in a fortnight seven lakh Buddhists and two lakh of the Aryas' land fell. The Buddhists made a wooden army by machines, which Indula burned with a fire arrow, and sent twenty thousand iron horsemen, whom Yogasimha shot down; Bauddhasimha made an iron lion that crushed Yogasimha, and a tiger that killed Bhogasimha after he killed the lion. Indula then bound ten thousand kings with a delusion weapon and crushed the machines; the heroes looted the palace, Bauddhasimha was freed by Jayanta and gave his daughter Padmaja to Jayanta and ten crore of gold to Ahlada, and the Buddhists swore never to enter the Aryas' land for a kingdom. The sages ask why Indula did not revive the dead; Suta says some came back from Yama's world, but Indra was told that Jayanta's reviving the dead broke the law of the worlds, so Indra withdrew the nectar-horse, and Indula, sad, worshipped Sharada and turned to yoga. Netrapala then gave ten crore of gold and the eight heroes went home with two lakh men.

07-030.json.summary: Suta says that while the heroes were in China, King Kamapala called Lakshana [nakula's part] to Kanyakubja, telling Jayachandra that on the seventh of Vaishakha's bright half Lakshana alone should come for his daughter or Prithviraj would seize him with an army. Lakshana goes with a hundred men, stays five days on the way, and is attacked by Padmakara and Prithviraj, but he knocks Prithviraj senseless and kills five hundred; Prithviraj then asks Padmakara to bind Lakshana for him, and Padmakara, greedy, gives him poison, binds him and hands him over, and Prithviraj has him put in prison. Padmini prays to Chandika, who tells Lakshana in a dream to repeat a mantra against all obstacles. In Ashadha Udayasimha and his companions, returning, miss Lakshana and, disguised as yogis (Dhanyapala with cymbals, Talana with a lute, Lallasimha with a drum), go to Parimala's court, where they sing, and then to Bindugadha, where Padmini sees through the disguise and weeps. Udayasimha dances at Prithviraj's gate in Dehli, and Prithviraj offers a boon; Udayasimha asks to see the king's iron prison, is shown, and is given wealth. Chandrabhatta tells Prithviraj of a dream in which Udayasimha says he will destroy the fire line and kill the Kaurava parts to establish Kali, and Prithviraj sends a thousand warriors to give Lakshana to Padmakara; Bhagadatta says that Padmini has a boon of invisibility, which she will use on Lakshana. Prithviraj swears by Mahadeva that Lakshana is not in his prison, and Udayasimha, believing him, goes grieving to Kamapala and then to Jayachandra, and faints. Svarnavati, as a parrot, with her servant Shobha and the spirit Mahamada, searches Kamarupa, Mayuranagara, Innagadha and Bahlika, where the god Markateshvara says he is powerless. After nine nights of fasting, Chandika tells Svarnavati that Padmini is the wife of the yaksha Manideva, Kubera's general slain by Bhima, who was promised by Mahadeva that she would have a husband of nakula's part in Vikrama's age, enjoy him, and, on losing him, return to Kailasa. Svarnavati goes to Padmini, who writes a letter to Parimala asking for help; Udayasimha besieges the city with twelve lakh; Kamapala and Padmakara fight, are made invisible by Padmini, and kill ten thousand men, until Udayasimha's divine sight lets him bind them and free Lakshana. They take Padmini home to Jayachandra, who rewards them and frees Kamapala, and the heroes are home in Jyeshtha.

07-031.json.summary: Suta says that the minister Chandrabhatta comes to the grieving Prithviraj, who asks when the thorns [Udayasimha and the others] will die. Chandrabhatta says Brahmananda, part of Arjuna, is Udayasimha's best friend, and when he dies all the gods' parts will go back where they came from. Prithviraj plans to call Brahmananda alone and kill him by trick, and sends the crafty king [Mahipati] to Mahavati, who tells Malana that Vela is now grown and has not been sent to her husband only because Udayasimha is held to be of low birth, so Brahmananda must come to Dehli or Vela will die. Parimala calls it a trap, but Malana threatens to die, and he lets his son go; Brahmananda goes with his uncle, then alone on Harinagara. In Dehli, on the eighth of Magha, seven wives of Vela's brothers (three widows and four with husbands) tell him that Vela killed their husbands and ask him to take them; he answers that wives were chaste in the Satya age, middling in Treta, lower in Dvapara and worst in Kali, and cites sages who allow widows to marry again in Kali; the widows adorn themselves and embrace him, but he refuses because his kin killed their husbands. They complain to Prithviraj, who calls him the lowest of kings and sentences him to prison; Brahmananda draws his sword and Prithviraj flees to Chamunda. The sages ask about the marriages of those women, and Suta tells, as earlier events, how the sons of Prithviraj were wed: Tarak to the daughter of Mayavarma of Anga, whom the demon Kitava had taken and who killed and ate her suitors; Tarak was seized and turned to stone, and Udayasimha's party killed Kitava, so Tarak was wed; then Nrihari wed Prabhavati, daughter of Mulavarma of Gurjara, and Udayasimha freed the couple from the yaksha Karabha; Saradana wed Madanavati of Kashmir after a gandharva war ended by Sharada; Mardana wed Suvela of Pundra after Ahlada woke the naga king Pundarika to get a naga ornament; Suryavarma wed Kantimati of Madra, then won her back from the rakshasa Karburu; Bhima wed Vidyunmala of Pattana, and Udayasimha's party drove back the king Bali's demons and the mleccha king Sahoda; Vardhana, who gained treasure from Kubera, wed Kinnari. Then, at thirty-one, Dhundhukara challenges Brahmananda, who burns half his army with a Brahma weapon. Prithviraj, advised by Mahipati and Chandrabhatta, sends Chamunda dressed as Vela in a palanquin with his four sons and Dhundhukara; on the eighth of Magha Chamunda stabs Brahmananda with a trident, the others strike him, and he cuts off the heads of Bhima, Vardhana and others before the rest flee. The true Vela finds him, he revives, and says that in the Kali age death is better than life, so they bathe at holy places in the east, south, west and north; at Gandhamadana he says he will leave his body on the eighth of Bhadra's bright half and asks her to kill Tarak, and she asks him to go to Kurukshetra and worship the goddess while she goes to Dehli and returns.

07-032.json.summary: Suta says that at thirty-two Vela, in yogi dress on Harinagara, comes to Mahavati and tells Parimala's court that Brahmananda was killed by trick, with Chamunda made to dress as a woman by Dhundhukara, and that he lies in a faint at Kurukshetra. The heroes curse the king and Malana, and each side sends letters; Vela writes an angry letter to Prithviraj. Prithviraj, losing sleep, calls all his kings and goes to Kurukshetra with twenty-four lakh men, parts of Dhritarashtra's sons; Parimala goes with sixteen lakh, as Drupada's part, and Vela, and camps at Syamantapanchaka. The chapter lists the kings who came to fight, with sons who are named parts of the Kauravas: Lahara and sixteen sons, Abhinandana of Bahlika and seven sons, Mayavarma of Anga and ten sons, Mulavarma of Gurjara, Kaikaya of Kashmir, Nagavarma of Pundra, Madrakesha, Purnamala of Magadha, and Mankana the Kinnara king with eight sons, and on the other side Netrasimha, Gajapati, Mayuradhvaja, Virasena, Lakshana, Talana, Dhanyapala, Lallasimha, Ahlada, Udayasimha, Jayanta and Jananayaka, with many lesser kings; the armies are explained by ranks and duties, and the war is said to last eighteen days. On the first days Udayasimha kills Lahara's sixteen sons and Chamunda's helpers in turn; Netrasimha and Gajapati kill each other; Udayasimha and Indula kill Mayavarma, his ten sons and others, and Virasena and Kamasena, and Nagavarma and his sons, fall in pairs and go to heaven in divine vehicles. Jananayaka's horse flies over the enemy; Mankana is bound by Jayanta; Netrasimha's and others' sons fall; Kuru-part kings Mulavarma, Purnamala, Kaikaya and Madrakesha die in battle. Lakshana kills Bhagadatta, but Chamunda and Tarak, in turn, kill Udayasimha and Devasimha and carry off Udayasimha's head, and Prithviraj holds a feast. Brahmananda, hearing of it, tells Vela to go to the field in his dress to kill Tarak; with Ahlada (Rama's part) at her side she fights Chamunda and Tarak, Ahlada crushes Tarak by wrestling, and Vela beheads him. Vela then builds a pyre and, with her father-in-law's leave, mounts it beside Brahmananda, and Indula's body is burned there too. Parimala, Dhanyapala and Talana are killed by Prithviraj's Rudra-given arrows, Lakshana's Vaishnava weapon fails against him and he is beheaded, and Malana and Devaki burn themselves. Kali appears with his wife and praises Ahlada; Ahlada asks that his fame spread and then, in a last fight, seizes Prithviraj by the hair and makes his eyes blue, so that Shiva leaves the king as impure. Ahlada goes with Kali to Gandhamadana to practise yoga. After sixteen years Prithviraj is attacked by Sahoddina, a mleccha, sent by Bali, who takes Vidyunmala and wealth; Jayachandra, hearing of his son's death, fasts and dies; Prithviraj is bound and, by his order, Chandrabhatta shoots him with an arrow and burns him.

08-001.json.summary: Vedavyasa speaks, saying that Suta has told the story of the sun and moon lines to the end of the Dvapara twilight; Suta will tell it again later at Vishala, as told by Vaitala, and the King Vikrama will call it again at Naimisharanya, and the eighteen Puranas will exist in the Kali age as upapuranas, with a twelve-chapter summary, the "Itihasasamuccaya". He adds that at the end of Vikrama's story comes a descent of Hari's part, the power-descent of Radha and Krishna, which Suta will tell the sages in eighty-eight thousand verses. The sages ask about the four fire-born lines of kings and how Hari, called three-age, was born in the Kali age. Suta first tells the Pramara line in the south: Pramara had a city built by Ambika; his son Mahamara ruled six years, then Devapi three years, then Devaduta. After Ashoka, the Buddhist king, was killed, Kali worshipped the Sun, who gave him a man named Shaka, and Kali gave him the city Taittira; Shaka overcame herdsmen and robbers and killed kings, so they were short-lived. Gandharvasena, Devaduta's son, ruled fifty years and went to austerity; his son Vikrama, by Shiva's order, ruled a hundred years and ten more were lost to the Shakas; Shalivahana, devoted to the gods' son, defeated the Shakas and ruled sixty years. A list of kings follows, each ruling like his father: Shalihotra, Shalivardhana, Suhotra, Havirhotra, Indrapala (who built Indravati), Malyavan (Malyavati). In Malyavan's time there was a four-year famine, the king cooked forbidden grain and offered it to the shaligrama, and a voice promised no famine while his line ruled. More kings follow: Shambhudatta, Bhumaraja, Vatsaraja, Bhojaraja, Bindupala, Rajapala, Mahinara, Somavarma, Kamavarma, Bhumipala, Rangapala, Virasimha, Kalpasimha (who built Kalapanagara), and Gangasimha, who died childless in battle at Kurukshetra at ninety, ending the line. The remaining Kshatriyas, the text says, mixed classes, took up Vaishya work and became like mlecchas.

08-002.json.summary: Suta says that Vayahani [Chapahani's line] ruled in the middle country and settled at Ajmer, which Brahma had made and Lakshmi (Rama) had entered, so that it is called "unborn". Tomara, his son, ruled ten years and worshipped Maheshvara for a year, and Shiva, pleased, gave him Indraprastha; the Kshatriyas born in his line are called Tomaras. Tomara's younger brother Samaladeva, then Mahadeva, Ajaya and Virasimha followed, each ruling like his father; Bindusura ruled fifty years, and his twins were a son and a daughter, Vira; the father gave Vira to Vikrama, with his realm. Next come Manikya, Mahasimha (fifty years), Chandragupta, his son, Mohana, Shvetaraya (thirty years), Nagavaha, Lohadhara, Virasimha, Vibudha, Chandraraya, Harihara, Vasanta, Balanga, Pramatha, Angaraya, Vishala, Sharngadeva, Mantradeva and Jayasimha, who conquered all the Aryan land and held a great sacrifice with the wealth. After him come Anandadeva and Someshvara; Anangapala's son wed Kirtimalini and had three sons, Dhundhukara, who ruled Mathura, Kumara, who took his father's seat, and Mahiraja, who ruled Dehli and died at the hands of the king Sahoddina. The Chapahani line is then said to end, its wives taken by mlecchas and piśachas, and the mixed offspring, called Jatta and Mehana, are said to be neither Arya nor mleccha, with a few Kshatriyas left here and there.

08-003.json.summary: Suta begins the Shukla line. When Krishna left the earth for his own place, divine Vrindavana, and Kali was about to arrive, the pious people on the islands were spoiled by Kali's friendship. Kali, with a mleccha woman, then ruled the islands for a very long time, worshipping the Sun; later he came to Bharata, was frightened to see it guarded by the world-guardians, and worshipped the Sun in meditation; after a hundred years the Sun, pleased, sent great rain, and the land became rich. A yavana named Nyuha fills the world. When the Kali age was a thousand years old Indra sent Kashyapa to Brahmavarta; with the goddess Aryavati he had ten sons, and after bringing the mlecchas of Mishra under control he settled between the Sarasvati and the Drishadvati, taught the eternal law of Manu to his sons and pupils, and sent his son Shukla to Raivata to worship Vasudeva, who showed him Dvaraka. After two thousand years Shukla, with three kinsmen and Brahmins, defeated the Buddhists at Mount Abu through its fire gate and rebuilt Dvaraka by Hari's grace; his son Vishvaksena, then Jayasena, Visena and others followed, with twins Pramoda and Modasimha, one daughter given to Vikrama. The lineage then runs through Sindhuvarma (Sindhu land), Sindhudvipa, Shripati (who won Kachchha, where a land bears his name), Bhujavarma (Bhuja land), Ranavarma, Chitravarma, Dharmavarma, Krishnavarma, Udaya, Vapyakarma (who built wells and tanks and fought King Balada), Guhila, Kalabhoja and Rashtrapala, each described as ruling like his father. Rashtrapala, through worship of Sharada, got the city Mahavati, guarded by Manideva, and had sons Vijaya and Prajaya. Prajaya, after twelve years of austerity on the Ganga, is told by the goddess in the form of a flute-playing girl on a horse to follow her blindfolded; when he opens his eyes he sees a city she made, Kanyakubja, named from the shape of its site; Jayapala ruled there ten years, his son Venuka (from the flute) wed Kanyavati, and they had seven daughters who are the mothers. Because of a woman's lapse by a well, the seven daughters turned to stone and Venu broke his vow of celibacy. The line continues: Yashovigraha, Mahichandra, Chandradeva, Mandapala (whom all kings left) and Kumbhapala, who bowed to the mleccha king Mahamoda and gave tribute; his son Devapala wed Chandrakanti, daughter of Anangapala, and had two sons, Jayachandra and Ratnabhanu; Ratnabhanu's son Lakshana died at Kurukshetra. The line of Kumbhapala, protector of Vaishyas, is said to end; the chapter closes by naming clans (Vishvaksena, Visena, Gauhila, Rashtrapala, Vaishyapala) descended from these kings and says the remaining small kings were of mixed class and spoiled by mlecchas.

08-004.json.summary: Suta tells the line of Parihara. Parihara, devoted to the Atharva Veda, defeated the Buddhists and, by worship of the all-powerful goddess, had her build a city half a yojana long on Chitrakuta hill, where Kali would be bound, so it is called Kalinjara; he ruled there twelve years. His son Gauravarma gave Kalinjara to his younger brother Ghoravarma and went to the Gauda land, where his descendants were Suparna, Rupana and Karavarma, then King Shaka, who worshipped Mahalakshmi, who after three years took the form of Kamakshi and lived there to protect her devotees, and Kamavarma ruled fifty years. His twins Bhoga and Bhogavati followed, and Bhogavati was given to Vikrama; Bhogavarma, and then Kalivarma, followed, and Kalivarma held a great festival for Mahakali, who gave him a boon and, by making many flowers, made a lovely city called Kalikata. A long run of kings follows, each ruling like his father: Kaushika, Katyayana, Hemavata, Shivavarma, Bhavavarma, Rudravarma and Bhojavarma (who founded Bhojarashtra), Gavavarma, Vindhyavarma (who went to Vanga), Sukhasena, Balaka, Lakshmana, Madhava, Veshava, Surasena, Narayana and Shantivarma, who built Shantipura on the Ganga; his son Nadivarma, with the Ganga's boon, built Nadiha in the Gauda land, a Vidyadhara protecting it; a Ganga line followed (Sharngadeva, Gangadeva, Ananga, Rajeshvara, Nrisimha). Kalivarma took Mahavati, and Dhritivarma ruled after; at Jayachandra's order a later king built Urvi city, and when the lunar Kshatriyas fell at Kurukshetra the king of Mahavati ruled twenty years until Sahoddina, the Kaurava parts dying at Kurukshetra. Ghoravarma, son of Parihara, ruled Kalinjara, and his son Shardula began the Shardula line, which is said to have spread over the earth by the great goddess's grace. Suta closes by saying he has told the line of the fire-born kings, and promises next how Hari himself was born.

08-005.json.summary: Suta tells that at midday of Brahma's day, at the turn of the Chakshusha period, a great wind shakes the golden mountain and the earth, the seven islands and seas turn to water, and only the Lokaloka mountain remains; after a thousand years the earth is under water. Vishnu, with Shiva and Brahma, makes the dolphin-shaped cycle of stars in the sky, and the earth, dried by the heavenly bodies, appears after ten thousand years. Brahma then creates Soma from his mouth as king of Brahmins, the Sun from his arms as king of Kshatriyas, the ocean from his thighs as king of Vaishyas, and Daksha, the skilled Vishvakarma, from his feet as king of Shudras; the four classes are said to descend from them. Vaivasvata Manu is born from the Sun's disc, and his period is counted as seventy-one divine ages. The chapter then tells of Vishnu's forms through the ages: Vishvarupa, Vamana and the three-age Narayana, in white Hamsa form in Satya, red Yajna in Treta and yellow Svarnagarbha in Dvapara; the life of men is four hundred years in Satya, three hundred in Treta, two hundred in Dvapara, and in Kali about a hundred for the righteous. At the Dvapara-Kali junction the parts of Vishnu and Vamana join and are born as Vasudeva and Devaki's son in Mathura. Vishnu tells the gods that in the Kali age he will take many forms, that at the subtle Vrindavana the Vedas will be gopis and play with him, and that at the end of the age, asked by Radha, he will end the play and become Kalki, bring the world's end, and restore the Satya dharma. Only Vishnu's devotees know this; the chapter closes with praise of Mahakali, Vishnu's maya, who makes and devours the world and becomes Mahagauri.

08-006.json.summary: The sages ask which kings came after Mahiraja, and Suta says that the pisacha Kutukoddina ruled Dehli and took Valigadha, a Yadava city, defeating Bhupasena, grandson of Virasena; kings from many lands drove him out, then Sahoddina returned, conquered them and destroyed images; many mlecchas then ruled five, six or seven years each, and within a hundred years they would be short-lived, weak destroyers of shrines, so Suta tells the sages to go with him to Vishala. They leave Naimisha, go to Vishala in the Himalaya, meditate on Hari, and after a hundred years go to Brahma's house. Manu then speaks, saying that ignorance had taken his knowledge and Brahman in the form of Vyasa raised him up, and asks what Suta did next. Vyasa answers with a teaching: the world is in the body; ego, the soul and Ishvara are described; Ishvara's eyes are the Shiva, Brahma, Vishnu and Bandha kalpas, his mouths the Vayu, Vahni, Brahmanda, Linga and Bhavishya kalpas, and his ten arms the Garuda, Bhagavata, Markandeya, Vamana, Narasimha, Varaha, Matsya and Kurma ones, as counted in Brahma's eighteen days, with the Kurma, Matsya and white Varaha kalpas first; Brahma is both subtle and gross, and his hundred-year life and day are measured in human years. By meditation the sages reach Satyaloka and stay a lakh of years, and on opening their eyes find men small, short-lived, mixed in class, with mlecchas and heretics everywhere, and the holy places and Vedas gone, becoming gopis with Hari. Suta then tells the "kalpa story" he saw in meditation: a mleccha king Timiralinga, of the Mukula line, comes to the middle country, kills many in Dehli, tells Brahmins they worship images and that shaligrama stones are worthless, burns them, loads the stones on camels, and makes seats of them at Taittira. The gods, who live in the shaligramas, complain to Indra, who hurls his thunderbolt, and the mleccha dies; the gods cast the stones into the Gandaki and go to heaven. Indra asks Brihaspati for help; Brihaspati says Vishnu gave Shachi a boon that he would be her son in Kali, that she will come in Gauda land near Shantipura on the Ganga, and that Indra should become a Brahmin; Indra, with the Rudras, Vasus and Ashvins, goes to Prayaga in Magha and pleases the Sun, and Brihaspati tells him the Sun's greatness in twelve chapters.

08-007.json.summary: The sages ask what Brihaspati taught of the Sun's greatness, and Suta says that Indra, at Prayaga, asked for it. Brihaspati tells how the Brahmin Dhatrisharma of Barhishmati, wanting children, pleased Prajapati and got a son, a daughter and a son; worried about their weddings and wealth, he worshipped Tumburu and then Kubera, who gave wealth and a yaksha knowledge that gives five kinds of gold. Near death, ill, he praised Shiva, who gave him knowledge, then worshipped the Sun with Sunday vows; in the fifth year the Sun, pleased, offered a boon, and after his hymn Dhatrisharma asked for liberation. The Sun lists four kinds of liberation: same world by austerity, nearness by devotion, same form by meditation, and union by knowledge; he granted him liberation for a Manu's period and gave light from his mouth to a devoted Brahmin woman, so Dhatrisharma was born again as Ishvara in the house of Kavyakara and became famous. Brihaspati's second story is of Mitrasharma of Mayavati, a poet who loved women; at the Kumbha festival at Gangadvara he met Chitrini, the twelve-year-old daughter of Kamasena, and both fainted; she worshipped the Sun, he recited the Aditya Hridaya twelve times daily through Vaishakha, and after a month the Sun gave the boon; her parents were told in a dream and married her to him, and the couple worshipped a Sun diagram on a copper plate with red flowers, lived a hundred healthy years and reached the Sun's nearness. Indra then sees the Sun with the gods, who says his part will be born on earth, and Ramananda is born at Kashi to Devala of Kanyakubja, abandoned by his parents, and Hari with fourteen parts lives in his heart. Third comes Aryaman, a Brahmin of the Satya age with wife Pitrimati and seven sons; he worshipped the Sun for a month in the Jyeshtha season, received a jewel that gives a measure of gold daily, built wells, tanks and houses for dharma, and after a thousand years went to the Sun's world, living there a lakh of years and taking the Sun's form. The gods praise the Sun in verse, and he appears and says that at the end of Dvapara Sudarshana will be born by Krishna's order as Nimbaditya to remove the decay of dharma: south of Meru by the Narmada in the Tailanga country, learning right dharma from Narada, then living at Mathura, Naimisha and Dvaraka. Sudarshana is born to Aruna of Bhrigu's line and Jayanti on the full moon of Kartika; one day Brahma comes hungry and asks for food while the sun is in the sky, the sun sets before he eats, and the sage holds the sun's light on a neem tree, so Brahma bows and names him Nimbaditya. The chapter ends here.

08-008.json.summary: Brihaspati continues telling Indra stories of the Sun's greatness. A Brahmin of Ayodhya, Shakrasharma, worshipped the Ashvins, Rudras, Vasus and Adityas with Yajurveda mantras, lived ten thousand years, became the Sun and, after a lakh years there, went to Brahma's world; Indra worshipped the Sun in Ashadha, and the Sun said he would be born at Vrindavana as Madhu, son of the Brahmin Madhava, who is Madhvacharya in the text. In Dvapara a farmer-Brahmin Meghasharma, whose field alone had rain during a drought in Shantanu's time, advised the king to have twelve Brahmins recite the Sun's mantra a lakh times in Shravana; rain came, Shantanu became a Sun devotee, Meghasharma lived five hundred years and became the Sun, and the Sun says he will be born at Vrindavana as Shridhara, son of Vedasharma, whose work on the Bhagavata is placed above the Purana. Prāṃśusharma, a truthful beggar Brahmin, met Kali disguised as a garden owner offering fruits; he refused them as fruit of the kalinda tree, in which Kali lives, unless first offered to the shaligrama, whereupon the fruit became like a shaved calf's head; Kali, as king, beat and jailed him, the Sun freed him and sent him to Kalinjara, where he lived a hundred and twenty-five years. The Sun then says he will be born at Kalinjara in the twenty-eighth Kali year as Vishnusharma [Vishnusvami], son of Shivadatta, who teaches that Vishnu is lord of all and should be worshipped after the gods as servants first greet the king's court. Next, Bhagasharma, son of an apsara and a sage, abandoned, worshipped the Sun for a hundred years, and the Sun says he will be born at Kanyakubja as Vanibhushana, who defeats meat-eating Brahmins and revives the fish they had eaten. A Brahmin of the Sarayu, whose son was revived by the Sun and named Vivasvan, forced a woman on Shivaratri, was struck with leprosy, was cured by Sunday vows, and became the Sun; the Sun says he will be born at Kashi as Karyaguna Dikshita, who learns from Shiva the allegory of the bull of grammar and defeats the Bhattas with the Siddhanta Kaumudi. Last, Ganaka, priest of King Satyadatta of Kanchi, advised a market day on which unsold goods were bought by the king; the king bought a poor man, whom he held in his treasury, and Karma and Dharma left until the man was released; Lakshmi herself stayed at the king's prayer, and Ganaka's son Pusha, who became the Sun, is to be born in Ujjayini as Mihiracharya, exposed in a river, reared by rakshasis and taught astrology in Lanka, then sent home by Vibhishana to restore astrology that the mlecchas had destroyed.

08-009.json.summary: Brihaspati continues to Indra. At the end of Treta, in Simhala island, King Parikshit's daughter Bhanumati served the Sun, who ate at her house; when she was bathing at Nalini lake on a Sunday, Narada took her cloth and asked for her hand, and she refused, saying she is human-born and his body is full of impurities beside the apsaras; Narada, ashamed, went to Shiva, and, though turned leprous, was healed when Shiva praised the Sun. Bhanumati and the Sun did austerity together, and the Sun says he will be Dhanvantari at Kashi, son of the Brahmin Kalpadatta, taking as pupil the prince Sushruta, so that diseases fade at his sight; Sushruta studies the hundred-chapter Kalpaveda and writes the Sushruta tantra. Helin of Pampapura, skilled in sixty-four arts, gave up gifts for craftsmen's work, made machines, spent his earnings on Magha sacrifices to the Sun as Vishvakarma, who accepted food at a pillar by the Pampa lake; the Sun says he will be born at Bilgrama in Vanga as Jayadeva, a poet. Jayadeva serves his parents twelve years, performs the Gaya rite, turns to renunciation, and at twenty-three, when a Brahmin offers his daughter Padmavati to Jagannatha, the god tells him to give her to Jayadeva. He composes the Nirukta and, the text says, Panini composed pure grammar to overcome the makers of vulgar speech. Kali's thieves later rob and cut off Jayadeva's hands and feet; Padmavati, grieving, lifts him from a pit; King Dharmapala finds him and takes him home. Kali's men, posing as Vaishnavas, show the king a false Vishnu, and slander Jayadeva as poisoning food; the king has him impaled and then cut again, until the thieves are exposed, dragged to Patala, and Jayadeva's limbs are restored. Brihaspati says next he will tell of Krishna Chaitanya.

08-010.json.summary: Brihaspati continues. A poor Brahmin, Vishnusharma, who had no son and lived by begging, was away when a wandering ascetic gave his wife a touchstone that turns iron to gold and left for three days; she made much gold, but her husband, seeing it, told her to go to people who enjoy wealth, saying he was afraid of thieves, and threw the stone into a drain. The ascetic, returning, asked for it, reproved him as poor and fooled by fate, and Vishnusharma showed him many pebbles in the drain that all looked like touchstones; the ascetic admitted that he had won the stone by twelve years of worship of Shiva and that greed had made him seek many, and he gained knowledge and liberation. Vishnusharma lived a thousand years, worshipped the Sun and gained union with Vishnu; the Sun tells Indra that in Phalguna he held Vishnu's light and heated the three worlds. Brihaspati tells Indra to worship that Sun in Phalguna; Indra does, and a four-armed red form comes out of the Sun's disc and enters Indra's body, so that Indra and Shachi, she in the form of a Brahmin woman, live together on the Ganga bank for a year, and Shachi conceives. On the twelfth of Bhadra's bright half, on a Thursday, Vishnu is born with all his parts, four-armed and red; the Rudras, Vasus and others praise him in verses naming him Krishna Chaitanya, son of Shachi, who comes in Kali to give devotion. The gods then ask Brihaspati how they will be born; he tells of a hunter-Brahmin, a killer of Brahmins, who was told by Marichi and the seven sages that his sin could not be shared with his family and, taught to repeat "mara mara", became Valmiki after a thousand years, wrote the Ramayana and later became Shiva. He then tells how, in the Vaivasvata age, Brahma at Utpalaranya made the four classes from his mouth, arms, thighs and feet, with Soma, Sun, ocean and Daksha as their kings, and Daksha's offering excluded Shiva, who in anger took the form of Virabhadra, struck down the gods, and made the sacrifice-spirit, a deer, flee until Brahma pacified him; Brahma set Shiva in the moon's disc for twenty-seven days. Virabhadra, pleased, sends a part of himself to be born in Kali as Shankara, son of the Brahmin Bhairavadatta, who writes the Shankara commentary, shows the Shaiva path, and makes the three-line mark, the rudraksha rosary and the five-syllable mantra. The chapter ends here.

08-011.json.summary: In Naimisha forest there was a Brahmin called Ajagara, skilled in Vedanta and a worshipper of Shambhu (Shiva). After twelve years Rudra was pleased by his clay-image worship and gave him knowledge. He praised the Lord, took the form of a serpent, and the creator later made him the moon. Shesha-Rudra then put forth his own radiance into a Brahmin's house in the Vindhya hills; the boy, called Girisharma, defeated scholars, came to Kashi and became a pupil of Shankara. The next account tells of Nairrita, a poor Brahmin of Prayaga who served Hari. The sage Narada asked Vishnu why his devotees are poor on earth. Vishnu explained a scheme of dharma and adharma, the seven upper worlds and the lower worlds and hells, and said that those who first honour the gods and then serve him become rich. Nairrita, who had left the gods, was poor. Narada offered a boon to the Brahmin's wife, who asked to be a queen; the Brahmin foolishly wished her to be a jackal, and the son wished his mother restored, so the three boons were used up. Narada then told him to worship Shiva; after a year Shiva gave him wealth like Kubera's. He later became Rudra-born Nairrita and a pupil of Shankara. Two more births are told: Vanasharma, who defeated scholars and joined Shankara, and Ajaikapada, son of Vasusharma of Mahishmati. He was given by Shiva as a gift of his own part, fought Death and his diseases, and was named Mrityunjaya. He too was born again as Purisharma and became Shankara's pupil.

08-012.json.summary: The chapter opens with the demon Hirbu (Hirbughna), of the Nikumbha line, who did austerities for a thousand years. Brahma offered a boon and he asked not to die at the hands of anything made by Brahma, moving or still. He then conquered heaven and the gods suffered for a hundred thousand years. Narada advised them to worship Shiva; after eleven years of clay-image worship Shiva appeared as a column of light and burned the worlds, destroying the demons and sparing the gods' devotees. Brahma and Vishnu praised Rudra, and Brahma set Hirbughna up as Maharudra, lord of the moon's sphere, for the gods' sake. The text then lists several births of Shiva's parts as pupils of Shankaracharya in Kashi, told by Brihaspati: Bharatisha (Hirbughna's rebirth), and the Maya-born ascetic who did austerities and for whom Brahma made three cities of gold, silver and iron. The gods, hungry and powerless, prayed to Vishnu, who took the Buddha form and misled the Vedic Brahmins. In the true age Shiva, worshipped on Kailasa, was given a chariot made from the essence of the earth, sun, moon and Meru, with Brahma as charioteer. Vishnu made the bow Pinaka, Shesha the string and Indra the arrow, and Shiva burned Tripura. Later births follow: Nathasharma (son of the yogi Macchanda and the nymph Rambha, a teacher of Gorakha), Kshetrasharma, and Aurva, the fire born from a sage's thigh, whose fierce radiance was thrown into water and drunk by a sea-mare. After this the text tells of the Goddess Prakriti in the single sea, who praised the Supreme with five mouths. From this came Svayambhu (Brahma), the goddess Mahalakshmi, and the dividing of the Lord into Ganesha and another four-armed form. Shiva worshipped Ganesha and praised him as remover of obstacles, asking him to be his son. Ganesha was born from Parvati's body on Kailasa. When Shani (Saturn) looked at the child at the festival, his head fell off. The gods blamed Shani, who put an elephant's head with one tusk on him, and Brahma took a crab's head for the elephant's womb. Ganesha later took birth in Kashi as Dhundhiraja, son of an astrologer Brahmin, wrote the astrology work Jatakabharana, and became a pupil of Shankaracharya. (One verse slot, number 63 in the source, is blank, and some verse numbers in the source are out of order.)

08-013.json.summary: This chapter tells how Brahma, after sixteen years on the lotus, desired his own daughter Sharada (born from his mouth), who rebuked him and vanished. His anger created the fierce Rudra Bhairava, who cut off Brahma's fifth head with his nails. Frightened, Brahma took refuge in Bhairava; a loud weeping followed and the falling tears grew into rudraksha trees. Shiva took the skull and was called Kapali; he was freed from the sin of killing a Brahmin only at Kashi, at the Kapalamochana tank. Bhairava was then born in Kashi as a renunciate, became Shankara's pupil and composed the Damara Tantra, opening mantras that had been locked. The account then turns to Mandodari, who worshipped Vishnu and withdrew into a Vindhya cave. Next it tells of Vishrava and Kaikasi, parents of Ravana and Kumbhakarna, who gained a boon from Brahma, conquered the gods, and were opposed by the gods' worship of Shiva. Shiva was born as Hanuman to Anjana, wife of the monkey Kesari, with the help of Vayu. As a child Hanuman went to seize the sun; Ravana was beaten by him in a wrestling bout. Brahma told Hanuman that Rama would be born in the 28th Treta age and that he would find fulfilment in devotion to him. Hanuman was born later as Balasharma, was beaten in debate by Shankara, and became his pupil, composing a tantra of many castes.

08-014.json.summary: The chapter begins with the origin of the world from the formless imperishable light, then the birth of Brahma from a lotus out of Virat's navel, and his questioning "Who am I?" Vishnu appeared as a child on his lap and claimed to be his father; Rudra then appeared as a fiery pillar and the two searched for its ends in vain, then praised him. The demon Tarakasura received a boon that only a son born of Shiva's seed could kill him, so the gods asked Shiva to marry. The story of Sati, Daksha's insult and her death is recalled, and then her birth as Parvati to Himalaya and Mena. Shiva refused to take a wife, so he gave his seed to Agni; at Brahma's request Vishnu created Pradyumna (Kama), whose arrows disturbed all beings and made Shiva yearn for the goddess. The goddess vanished, then offered marriage with her parents' consent; the Seven Sages arranged the wedding. The chapter lists her names (Uma, Katyayani, Gauri, Kali, Bhavani, Durga, Chandika). Kama was burned by Shiva's anger and became bodiless (Anangaka); his wife Rati, after worship, was promised he would be born as Pradyumna, son of Krishna. The text then reports a long debate: Shiva's part was born as Ramanuja's brother in Godavari region, and Rama-sharma lost to Shankara. The Vaishnava Ramanuja then won debates on Vedanta, grammar, Mimamsa and logic by showing Hari as supreme, and Shankara became his pupil under the name Govinda. It closes with the fruit of hearing.

08-015.json.summary: Sumantu starts the story of wealth and Shiva's glory. Yakshasharma, a wicked Brahmin, was afflicted with leprosy but by chance kept a Shivaratri fast and died in a temple; he was reborn as King Rajaraja of Karnata, a devotee of Shiva, who later became the Rajarajeshvara light-pillar. Reborn from Ilvala as Kubera, he received golden Lanka from Brahma, became lord of Yakshas, Kinnaras and Guhyakas, and the giver of wealth. Ravana drove him out; Kubera took shelter with Shiva and got Alakavati. Ravana was cursed by Suprabha when he touched Nalakubara's wife; he worshipped Shiva, offered his heads and bodies in fire, and by Brahma's boon did not die. The gods, hungry without sacrifices, went to the milk ocean; Vishnu said he would act through Sita and Rama, a form of Hari. Sita was born from the earth; Rama, Lakshmana, Bharata and Shatrughna are described as forms of Vishnu and his emblems. After a thousand years of rule Rama gave the Pushpaka to Kubera and went on. The chapter then tells that Kubera was born as the merchant Trilochana of Mathura, who became Ramananda's pupil. Rama served in his house for thirteen months, gave gifts, and then told him he was Rama, not a servant, and would live in his heart. Trilochana left his family and meditated on Rama by the Sarayu. The chapter ends there, with the account of Trilochana unfinished.

08-016.json.summary: The chapter tells the birth stories of some of the eight Vasus as later teachers. First, King Prachinabarhi gave up animal sacrifice on Narada's advice and had ten sons, the Prachetas, who practised austerities in the sea; one of them, Apava, is identified with Varuna.
